In the third session, we'll go into some advanced concepts in SQL.
For example, you can use some MySQL tools for organizing your code a little more.
A User Defined Function or a UDF is something you have available in MySQL.
You can use it to define functions for uses that aren't already readily available in MySQL through the standard SQL functions.
A stored procedure can be used to store code you find yourself running quite regularly with some changes here and there.
For example, let's say you have to run a given query daily for a daily report.
You can store this as a stored procedure and parameterize it so that it's also customizable, and every day when you run it, by varying a few inputs, you can make it answer the query that is most important to you that day while not having to write your code from scratch every day.
We'll also look at some tips and tricks for query optimization. In other words, tips and tricks that help you write more efficient queries that help you get to the answer of that business question more efficiently.
For any operation that requires you to search a big database, it helps to make an index in MySQL.
You will learn how many types of indexes you have available in SQL, and you will also learn how to make them and where to use them.
You'll also look at some best practices for coding that will help you further tune the readability and reusability of your code.
We will spend some time looking at the order in which the SQL compiler executes the different clauses of the SELECT statement.
Having this understanding will help us understand how the SQL compiler works, and it will help us tune our queries more to the point that they are very efficient, and the SQL compiler has a very easy job running them efficiently.
We'll close out by looking at joins vs. nested queries and comparing them for efficiency so we get a better sense of which one to prefer for what type of analysis.

USER DEFINED FUNCTIONS (UDFs) - INTRODUCTION What are UDFs? - Similar to UDFs in other programming languages, such as Python - MySQL UDFs do the following: - Accept parameter(s) - Perform action(s), such as a complex calculation - Return the result of the above action as a value Why use UDFs? - Ability to define functions not available directly in SQL - Improves code readability UDFs - EXAMPLE Syntax: /* Function Definition */ DELIMITER $$ CREATE FUNCTION function_name(func_parameter1, ) RETURNS datatype [characteristics] BEGIN <MySQL statements>; RETURN expression; END; $$ DELIMITER ; /* Function body must contain one RETURN statement */ Example: /* Function Definition */ DELIMITER $$ CREATE FUNCTION age_today(release_date date) RETURNS INT deterministic BEGIN RETURN year(current_date) - year(release_date); END; $$ DELIMITER ; /* Viewing Output */ SELECT mov_id, movie_title, age_today(movie_main.release_date) AS movie_age FROM movie_main;

395.text: UDFs has limited uses. So for example, it can only replace SQL functions or in other words, it can only be used in ways a built-in SQL function would have been used. For example, we've declared this function, age_today, and what it does is it calculates the age of a movie, it finds out how many years it has been since the movie was released. And we've used it in pretty much the same way we would have used a built-in SQL function such as CONCAT, or UPPER, or ABS, or something like that. But this is really the only use you can have out of a UDF. UDFs will not execute code blocks or code batches for you. They cannot be used to perform tasks such as updating age column here in the actual source table, or adding really this column to the source table. They'll only ever be used in querying the data, selecting something, and, and showing that to your screen. But if you recall, in Python, for example, you do have a lot of functions that don't necessarily return a set type of value but can just perform some actions and do a bunch of other things. And so that's where stored procedures come in. Stored procedures are this other type of stored routines in SQL that let you do all of these other things that a UDF cannot do. Perform actions, etc., and, and, and all of the other stuff that you would have wanted to execute. What is a stored procedure? So, essentially, it's just an object file in SQL that stores the code block that you want to keep running repeatedly. And so, essentially, just by saving a object file as a stored procedure, you can then run the code block within it with or without parameters repeatedly. For example, here we've used a stored procedure to output movies in the movie_main table that have age less than 20 years on the current date. So, to do that, we've defined this stored procedure, output_movies_with_age_less_than. And just like UDFs, the actual definition for this procedure, output_movies_with_age_less_than, should be written before you write the call statement. Also, just like for UDFs, you declare your delimiter change, and you will end with sort of resetting the delimiter to the semicolon, and between all of these, between these two keywords is where you'll write the procedure. You'll say, "Create Procedure", and then declare the procedure's name and say what input parameters you're going to be using, and then between the BEGIN and END keywords, you'll be writing the main body of your procedure.

397.text: Let's now look at some more differences between stored procedures and UDFs. So if you might recall, uh, UDFs are sort of very specific functions. They uh let in some parameter or some column and will give you as output something that can be used as a SQL column. So, they are similar to your existing SQL functions in usage such as UPPER, LOWER, CONCAT, and ABS. Uh and but that's the really the only functionality they are available for. A stored procedure is available to you for general purpose use. Uh the usage can be not just returning a column, for example, but updating it or doing something else, performing an action that doesn't neatly fit into sort of your standard SQL function format. Uh and so for that reason, stored procedures are able to uh not really ask you to return a value. They give you the option to either return it if that's something you want, or not really return it. Uh but for a UDF, it is mandatory to return something. Uh so you can use it in your SQL columns. Uh they are also different in how they are uh how they approach compiling and execution. A stored procedure is only compiled once uh and then it's just executed whenever it's called. Uh so it's a little efficient in sort of how it uses its runtime. Uh but user defined UDFs are actually compiled every time they are called or executed. A stored procedure can call a function within itself and a UDF is not really able to call a procedure. It can call a function but not really a procedure. Uh and again, a UDF can only use the SELECT clause, but with a stored procedure, you have sort of a variety of DDL or DML statements available, you SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, pretty much everything that uh you would usually use, you have available in in a stored procedure. Some more things you can do in stored procedures, for example, that you cannot do in UDFs is, you can use try-catch blocks to find out where the errors or exceptions are and then uh in advance sort of plan for them in stored procedures. You can use a CTE within your definition body in a stored procedure and not so much in a UDF. Uh and a stored procedure lets you define input or output parameters, uh but a UDF can only let you define input parameters.

As you might recall, we said that it helps for a table to have an index if you know that there is a column you're going to be looking up a lot and you sort of need that lookup to be efficient. When I say lookup, I mean something like, when I say I want to print all movies from the table movie_main where language is English. So I'm sort of just basically looking up in the column language for English language movies. So, again, we did say that indexing that column does make that lookup more efficient. Let's see why that is. So, for example, let's say I want to just output rows from this table that are English language movies. In this scenario, where this table is not sorted by the column language, but by some other column, I will have to do a lot of search operations. Basically, the compiler will have to compare for each row the value of language to English and check whether any of them match. And sort of this will have to be done for every single row in the table, from start to finish. But consider a scenario where the table itself is sorted by the language column. Here, if I ask for the same query to be run, I again just ask for all of the rows from this table where the language is English, it just has to keep searching until it finds a language different than English. So there are some best practices that are always suggested to keep your SQL code readable.
Following these will help other people quickly look at your code and figure out what's going on without you having to explain it a lot.
But more importantly, it will also help you sort of figure out what's going on.
Let's say a year down the line, or a few months down the line you look back at your own code, it might not be as obvious to you as it is right now as to what the code is doing.
But if you follow certain best practices and keep the code easy to read, it will be sort of easy for you to quickly ascertain that.

So the number one best practice is always to write appropriate comments.
The trick here is to not overdo it but write enough comments that you sort of get a general idea of what's going on.
If there's something that you feel needs to be called out so it's not that obvious and somebody would help from knowing it, it's always a good practice to sort of write that as a comment there.

You should also always use table aliases for SQL statements that involve more than one source.
So for example, let's say your query has a join and it's joining more than one table to get to that final table that it then selects from.
It always helps for each column to use table aliases, so it's easy to see which table each of those columns are coming from.
It also in general while writing the join itself helps you to have those aliases in case the tables have very big names.
We'll look at examples for a lot of these shortly, but that's the general idea for the second best practice here.

It also always helps to just assign very simple descriptive names for the columns and tables in your data set.
Don't make them very long and while they are short they should be able to convey swiftly and efficiently and correctly what the column is supposed to be or what the tables are supposed to be doing in your data set.

So the fourth one here is a big one. Any SQL keyword you ever use should be all in capital letters.
So for example, keywords such as FROM, WHERE, JOIN, SELECT. These should always be in capital letters and any names of columns, tables, or variables.
So for example, things like collisions, party age, movie main and gross et cetera, things like those in our examples, they should always be in lowercase.
Writing your query this way, keeping some parts of it in uppercase and some parts in lowercase will help you very very quickly, very visually figure out which part of your query is doing what and it does help you comprehend everything much quicker than if you weren't following these best practices.

It also helps if you maintain the right level of indentation for different sections of a query.
So what that means is let's say you have a complex query that involves a lot of SELECTs and FROMs and JOINs.
Indenting it the right way can sometimes go a long way in figuring out really quickly what is being selected from what table and what's being joined and we'll look at examples of that very shortly.

It also helps to use new lines for different sections of a query.
So if you are, for example, using multiple joins, then it helps to sort of have each of those in new lines and not in just the one same line just so that the code is a little more readable.

The last one is also a very important one.
So in your SELECT clause, let's say you have five columns, instead of writing all of them in one line and separating them by commas, it again helps to just write all of these column names in different lines.
So they are using up five lines and it's a little easier for you to figure out again what each of those columns is that you're trying to get from your source table.

A lot of these tips are best practices because SQL, unlike Python, will run even if you don't use the right indentation or the line breaks or everything, and even if you don't follow sort of the right cases.
SQL will still run the code without an error and give you the same answer, but it does help to be following all of these best practices so it's easier for you, again as stated earlier, to figure out what's going on in your code.

But more importantly, it will also help you sort of figure out what's going on. Let's say a year down the line, or a few months down the line you look back at your own code, it might not be as obvious to you as it is right now as to what the code is doing. But if you follow certain best practices and keep the code easy to read, it will be sort of easy for you to quickly ascertain that. So the number one best practice is always to write appropriate comments. The trick here is to not overdo it but write enough comments that you sort of get a general idea of what's going on. If there's something that you feel needs to be called out so it's not that obvious and somebody would help from knowing it, it's always a good practice to sort of write that as a comment there. You should also always use table aliases for SQL statements that involve more than one source.

You should also always use table aliases for SQL statements that involve more than one source. So for example, let's say your query has a join and it's joining more than one table to get to that final table that it then selects from. It always helps for each column to use table aliases, so it's easy to see which table each of those columns are coming from. It also in general while writing the join itself helps you to have those aliases in case the tables have very big names. We'll look at examples for a lot of these shortly, but that's the general idea for the second best practice here. It also always helps to just assign very simple descriptive names for the columns and tables in your data set. Don't make them very long and while they are short they should be able to convey swiftly and efficiently and correctly what the column is supposed to be or what the tables are supposed to be doing in your data set. So the fourth one here is a big one. Any SQL keyword you ever use should be all in capital letters. So for example, keywords such as FROM, WHERE, JOIN, SELECT. These should always be in capital letters and any names of columns, tables, or variables.

So for example, keywords such as FROM, WHERE, JOIN, SELECT. These should always be in capital letters and any names of columns, tables, or variables. So for example, things like collisions, party age, movie main and gross et cetera, things like those in our examples, they should always be in lowercase. Writing your query this way, keeping some parts of it in uppercase and some parts in lowercase will help you very very quickly, very visually figure out which part of your query is doing what and it does help you comprehend everything much quicker than if you weren't following these best practices. It also helps if you maintain the right level of indentation for different sections of a query. So what that means is let's say you have a complex query that involves a lot of SELECTs and FROMs and JOINs. Indenting it the right way can sometimes go a long way in figuring out really quickly what is being selected from what table and what's being joined and we'll look at examples of that very shortly. It also helps to use new lines for different sections of a query.

It also helps to use new lines for different sections of a query. So if you are, for example, using multiple joins, then it helps to sort of have each of those in new lines and not in just the one same line just so that the code is a little more readable. The last one is also a very important one. So in your SELECT clause, let's say you have five columns, instead of writing all of them in one line and separating them by commas, it again helps to just write all of these column names in different lines. So they are using up five lines and it's a little easier for you to figure out again what each of those columns is that you're trying to get from your source table. A lot of these tips are best practices because SQL, unlike Python, will run even if you don't use the right indentation or the line breaks or everything, and even if you don't follow sort of the right cases. SQL will still run the code without an error and give you the same answer, but it does help to be following all of these best practices so it's easier for you, again as stated earlier, to figure out what's going on in your code.

Hello friends, welcome to this session. We are in the last stages of our course. We have already covered important topics such as importance of data collection, importance of validity, importance of measurements. And now, I think we are in a position to now understand the importance of principles of data management and analysis. Today, we are going to cover two areas: one, database management, the other one, on data analysis strategy.

Data management includes the following: Defining variables, creating study database and data dictionary (about which I am going to expand), entering the data and correct the errors, create a dataset for data analysis, backing up the data and archiving the dataset. Today, we are going to cover the key elements of data management including data structure, data entry, individual and aggregated databases, mother and daughter databases.

What is data structure? For some of you who may be new to the word database, this is an example of a database. Each of these lines, these horizontal lines, represent records, pertaining to one particular individual. Each of these columns represent a variables, the information that is collected on certain variables based on the study question.

Data documentation: We need to initially formulate the entire plan of how the data is going to be managed. That can come in the form of what is called data documentation. It can talk about the structure, meaning the name, number of records, etc., and other relevant information about the structure. The variables in terms of the name, what values that are assigned to, the coding, etc., and the history of this database in terms of when it was created, when it was modified, the storage related information, in which media it is going to be stored, where and how it is going to be backed up, and any other relevant additional information. These are recorded in terms of the structure.

Identifier in the database: Let's look at the first of the important elements in database. This is called identifier. This identifier has to be unique, and that's why it's called unique identifier. It is maintained by a computerized index, and this particular unique identifier has to be secured by a procedure, quality assurance procedure that guarantees that each of these data has its own internal validity.

The code can comprise information that will talk about that particular individual. For example, it can have 7 digits. Each of these digit, or set of digits, can refer to a specific identifier information about that particular individual about which about whom the data was collected. For example, in this example, the first and the second digit can denote the village or area. The next set of two digits, the third and fourth, may denote street. The digit number 5 may indicate the house or, you know, flat or residence, door number. The last two digits can denote the person's sequential number. Therefore, this 7-digit may represent the about that particular individual. And by parts, it can give information.

Structure of the variables in the database: You need to specify certain things about variables. The variable, as you might have seen in the lecture on measurement, there are different types of variables that do exist and therefore it requires your attention in the beginning itself. You need to specify whether the variable will be entered as digits or if it is a numeric, whether the number of decimals are important. The variables can be entered as length, in which case, you need to specify the length. And it is preferable that when you are entering as both text and number, you turn all the letters into capitals to avoid errors, which can cause a lot of problem in data analysis. And finally, you can have dates in a specific format. When I say specific format, you need to specify whether it is entered as the Indian format date, month, and year in 4 digits, or month, month, date, and then year. This has to be specified in the structure of the variable.

Creating variable names: While creating the variable names, which pertain to your data collection instrument about which you will have a clear idea later part of the course, you need to be very clear. The name, variable name should refer to an item in your data collection instrument. It has to be understandable format. For example, if the questionnaire item is about exercising, whether the individual exercises daily or not, the variable name could be EXERDAILY, Exercise Daily. That clearly denotes what questionnaire item it refers to.

The second important criteria is in terms of keeping it short, leaving no space between the between the letters of the variable name. Most softwares may require less than 10 characters, therefore you have to be very choosey at the same time it is self-explanatory. The third important aspect is: be consistent. For example, for different types of response to a question on how frequently somebody exercises: Exercising daily in the past can be denoted by EXERPAST, Exercise Past, that clearly, you know, self-explanatory about that particular questionnaire item. If it is currently daily, then it is coded accordingly. If it is past occasionally, the words are given in the variable name, so that by looking at the variable name, the investigator can easily identify, okay, this is the variable this is the questionnaire item it refers to. And finally, you may have variables collected as such. These are called crude variables. For example, it it may refer to number of times one exercises. It could be three times, four times, five times a day. And finally, you may decide to regroup them into two categories: exercised or not. In which case, you can denote that variable as exercise in the crude variable as such when the data was collected. You can change it to exercise_12, which denotes its dichotomized. It is dichotomized into exercised or not. So, you have to be consistent in the pattern by which you create variable names. And finally, it's very important that you assign a variable name. Otherwise, if the software is left to assign a variable name by itself, it can create a lot of confusion, including duplicates of similar items within the questionnaire.

Design data entry-friendly data collection instrument: When you are designing a data collection instrument about which my my colleague is going to expand in the later part of this course, it is important that the design itself, you are very clear about broad sections of the questionnaire, so that when it is converted into a database, you know that there are sections that you have to enter. For example, there is a section called identifiers. There is a section called, you know, demographics, which means, you know, one talks about age, gender, community, and family-related issues. And then the third section called outcome. It's about the problem in the question and or disease if it is related to typically clinical related information. And finally, another section called exposure, in which you can talk about all the variables that you are going to measure including what Dr. Tarun might have already talked to you about, third factors, including confounders. Finally, the instrument should allow an auto-coding. If you collect information on exercise daily, yes-no, if it is already written as 1-2, we need to enter into the database 1 or 2. We don't have to code it again. So, that's what is meant by auto-coding. So, the data collection instrument should be designed in a way that it facilitates data entry design easy.

Coding: An important aspect of data entry is all about coding. It's always preferable to have a numerical coding. Of course, you would have seen if it is textual information in the form of qualitative, there is a different way of dealing with it, but with reference to this session, we are talking about a quantitative data analysis, so it's preferable to have numerical coding. In particular, you need to decide on how you will code missing values. It could be in the form of a dot or depending on the field, you may choose to enter as 999, 999. Be careful, you don't enter, you know, the missing value for age is 99, that can mean differently. And if it is not applicable, you enter with a with a consistently with a particular coding in the data collection instrument. For beginners, with inadequate experience in handling databases, it's advisable don't create cumbersome codes. This is equally advisable for senior researchers. For example, if you have a field: Do you walk everyday? Walking as a variable. Do you cycle everyday as another questionnaire. You have two variable names, walking and cycling. Do you do both? And then there is a coding. And somebody very innovatively thought, walking and cycling if somebody is engaged, we will give a coding as 12, which is basically 1 and 2 combined. But that's not going to be helpful when you analyze information. And last, but very important, this is very critical, because most of the times we may be dealing with the dichotomized variables, so you need to be very clear that you are going to give 1 for yes, 0 for no, or 1 for yes, 2 for no, or 1 for present and 2 for absent, as a baseline for all the gradients. Some of the softwares have a different understanding of this 1 and 0, so when it comes to analysis, so you need to be careful about your software-related details also.

Constructing a data dictionary: Finally, when it comes to data entry, you need to have what is called the catalogue. Before the data entry is made, you create what is called data dictionary or variable catalogue, in which you talk about each of these variables, which questionnaire item it refers to, what are the variable values that will be assigned to this variable, what is the meaning of the each of these value in a particular format. Some of the softwares generate on their own this data dictionary as a catalogue, variable catalogue, but then it is preferable that you develop your own data dictionary for your study. In which, you refer first to the question item, the variable name that you have given, the type of variable, the format in which data is collected, the values that are assigned to, and some logical checks if any. This is written so that if this database is shared with the others, the person can make use of the data dictionary and can do the analysis on his or her own. It is equally important for you if you, after some time has lapsed, you go back to the database, it gives you an idea what you have done and what is the what is it all about for each of these variables, and it helps you later when you want to analyze your data again.

Check specifications before data entry: Before data entry, one makes sure that there are checks and balances. This is also very important from ensuring internal validity. You specify minimum and maximum values that can enter into a particular field. For example, if your study is about children up to 5 years, the age column will not entertain anything more than 5 years at the time of data entry itself. So that it it minimizes the errors that can come in even at the time of data entry. So that these will be acceptable at the time of entry. You may specify skip patterns. For example, if you ask a question "Do you exercise?" and that person says "No", then you can skip a lot of questions about type of exercise, frequency, nature, intensity, and things like that. So skip patterns are very useful, even at the time of data entry. And then of course, we talked about automatic coding. When you enter that code, it automatically denotes something that is referred to in the data collection instrument. That can be analyzed immediately. There may be certain times need for copying data from the preceding record. You know, for example, lab results if they have to be carried forward to another section, it it can get copied by itself. This can be specified in the database. And finally, some calculations. For example, you may collect height and weight data, but you may not calculate body mass index by your own in the data collection instrument, you can ask the database to do it when you enter height and weight, it automatically calculates BMI. So, these specifications are necessary before data entry is made.

Data entry: While you enter the data, it is important that we see these as an opportunity for cleaning the database. For example, you enter a data and you find that there are some notes that need to write. There are some clarifications that you need because you don't think that that is appropriate, so it serves a purpose of cleaning. The data entry person refers this back to the investigator for additional inputs to cleanly clean up the data. You can use checks while entering the data, which we also discussed as an automated check within the database. You have to mark each paper as and when the data entry is completed so that the duplicates are not entered. And after the data is entered, you may have to validate by different means. So, therefore, data entry is one step in the clean data cleaning aspect.

Individual and aggregated databases: We talked about individual and aggregated databases. We showed you a database, that is an individual database. Each record in the horizontal line is an observation. There could be instances in which you may have aggregated databases, where you may enter counts in each of the records. If you enter only one count by record, that is ideal, that is called normalized database because normalized database in which each of the rows contain only one count for that particular record, it facilitates aggregation by a vertical. I will show you what it is.

Aggregating individual data: For example, on the left-hand side, you see an example of individual data about people in whom place, age, gender, and onset. So, each of these records indicate an individual, and at the same time we can have aggregate data. For example, by place, one can also get number of people affected, number of people having problem, and things like that. So, this is an aggregated data by place, whereas the the red color database shows the individual data.

Mother and daughter databases: There can be an instance in which you may have what is called mother and data daughter database. You may collect information at various levels. You may collect information at the village level. You may collect information at the household level. You may collect information at the individual in the household. You may collect within an individual information about several episodes of illness or different problems in that individual using different questionnaire. So, in essence, you may have information about different levels. That doesn't mean, you know, you repeat the information in all the levels for that particular individual. For example, for that individual, you write information about the house. For that individual, you write information about the village. Not necessary. You can keep them at their level, and then at the time of data analysis, you can link the database that comes from village with database that comes from household. You can link the database that comes from household to the individual, so that you can sensibly analyze, you don't have to worry about keeping everything together and get confused at the time of data analysis. For example, this is a household level data, where you have information about the house ID, location, the house as such, its community status, and its income. The individual in the house may have information pertaining to whether they have a disease or not or they are exposed to a particular factor or not. So, you can see here, the house ID is repeated here, the person ID for that particular first household is indicated here, and diseased or not or exposed or not here. These are two different databases entered differently. One is a household database, another is the individual house database. We can link them as and when necessary using this connection called house ID, which is common to both the databases. There is a procedure by which we can do this in softwares. You can even merge these files if needed.

Summing up on data management: We need to code databases numerically. We need to enter data using quality assurance procedures which I outlined. You need to store information at the level where it needs to be stored, and we can relate or merge files when needed and as required. Thank you very much.

Some of the softwares have a different understanding of this 1 and 0, so when it comes to analysis, so you need to be careful about your software-related details also. Constructing a data dictionary: Finally, when it comes to data entry, you need to have what is called the catalogue.

Constructing a data dictionary: Finally, when it comes to data entry, you need to have what is called the catalogue. Some of the softwares generate on their own this data dictionary as a catalogue, variable catalogue, but then it is preferable that you develop your own data dictionary for your study. In which, you refer first to the question item, the variable name that you have given, the type of variable, the format in which data is collected, the values that are assigned to, and some logical checks if any. This is written so that if this database is shared with the others, the person can make use of the data dictionary and can do the analysis on his or her own.

It is equally important for you if you, after some time has lapsed, you go back to the database, it gives you an idea what you have done and what is the what is it all about for each of these variables, and it helps you later when you want to analyze your data again. You specify minimum and maximum values that can enter into a particular field. For example, if your study is about children up to 5 years, the age column will not entertain anything more than 5 years at the time of data entry itself. You have to mark each paper as and when the data entry is completed so that the duplicates are not entered. And after the data is entered, you may have to validate by different means. So, therefore, data entry is one step in the clean data cleaning aspect. Individual and aggregated databases: We talked about individual and aggregated databases. We showed you a database, that is an individual database. Each record in the horizontal line is an observation. There could be instances in which you may have aggregated databases, where you may enter counts in each of the records. For example, by place, one can also get number of people affected, number of people having problem, and things like that. You can link the database that comes from household to the individual, so that you can sensibly analyze, you don't have to worry about keeping everything together and get confused at the time of data analysis. For example, this is a household level data, where you have information about the house ID, location, the house as such, its community status, and its income. These are two different databases entered differently.

00:58 The data analysis strategy has its sequence, and I am going to talk about these seven steps. The first step is identifying the study type, which is essential before you venture into data analysis. The second is in terms of identifying main variables. The third, becoming familiar with the data. Fourth, characterize the study population, and fifth, examining the association between exposure and outcome based on the study type, and sixth, in terms of creating additional tables, and finally, to conduct an advanced analysis.

01:37 1. Identify study type
- Establish main analysis framework
- Descriptive study {Estimation of a quantity}
- Analytical study {Testing hypotheses}
- Get familiar with the study
- Review protocol for study objectives and study type
- Review questionnaire
- Review analysis plan
- Review data collection procedures
- Obtain electronic database(s)
- Decide on the software for analysis*

01:38 Identifying a study type is the first and foremost step before you enter into data analysis, because it establishes the main framework. I'm going to repeat again that you need to know whether you are dealing with a descriptive question or descriptive study, or you are dealing with an analytical study. If a descriptive study is involved, you need to measure a quantity and estimate appropriate indicator, which I'm sure you will have seen in the measurements lecture. And if it is an analytical study, you need to test hypothesis using statistical tests. For that clarity, you need to be familiar with the study. You need to look at the protocol, especially for study objectives and study type. You need to review the entire questionnaire, you need to look at the analysis plan, you need to look at the data collection procedures, you need to obtain the electronic database, and you may have to decide on software for analysis, about which we'll see at the end.

02:34 Analysis plan depends on objectives and study type

Analytical = Compare 2 groups

- Perform

- All the variables describing the study population

This will give you a fairly good idea of what this dataset is all about. And secondly, you review the observations by its status in the database. Are there duplicates? Cross check. Look for missing observations. Check the ranges and legal values against the specified, that was specified in the data dictionary. Check for consistency in the pattern of the data. So this is a crucial step, the third step, which you need to spend a sufficient time.

- Baseline characteristics
- Distribution of study participants by socio-demographic- economic variables
- e.g., Age, gender, income

- Based on a priori hypotheses
- Compare groups for frequency of exposures using appropriate measure of association
- Based on prior knowledge

- e.g., Creation of new variables

- Dose-response
- Stratifications
- Multivariate analysis

- Use empty table shells to prepare analysis

- Recoding

- Analytical

06:51 Some practical tips that you may want to keep in your notes: in terms of a prior plan of analysis, it's very useful. It has to be done. The data analysis has to be planned, plan has to be prepared well in advance. We will recommend you to use empty tables to prepare analysis. In your reading material, you will see such empty tables. For each of the study designs, we have prepared an empty table shell. So for your study, you can prepare a plan of action for analysis. Okay, this is how my table will look like. And then at the time of analysis, your attempt is to fill up that empty shells. The second step tip is in terms of analyzing it by stage. Go by stages. You first do the recoding that is necessary. You may create new variables, you may dichotomize, you may look at the descriptive information, you may decide to change the way you cut the two groups. You may decide on three or four groups for measuring dose response based on your understanding from the data. You may do the next step of descriptive analysis and then finally analytical analysis. So this has to be a sequential process, you should not jump. People have the tendency to jump the steps, but I think it has to be in a measured manner one by one. And finally, please avoid any analysis that is driven by the data that you analyze without any plan. This is called post hoc analysis. You did not have a plan, you finally find something and then you try to make news out of it. Last but very important, you don't squeeze out the data because you want something.

08:42 Initial stages of the analysis:
e.g., Effect of brisk walking on fasting blood sugar levels in diabetics

- Create outcome data
- Recode key variables e.g., age-groups, income

e.g., Effect of brisk walking on fasting blood sugar levels in diabetics
- Univariate analysis

- Frequency of outcome by income, stratified for age, gender and income
- Multivariate analysis

- Use software with data management & analysis tools

We think that it's a small dataset, let me use it in a spreadsheet, but I think we recommend that you better avoid that temptation because spreadsheets are not meant to be data management or data analysis tools per se. 00:00 This is the public sector data science course, where we teach data-related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

00:11 As part of the set of modules on everyday data science, today we will look at the basic functions in Excel that can help you prepare for a review of the scheme or program that you're working on. 

00:25 Within the broader module on basic Excel skills, in this session, we'll be learning about cleaning data downloaded from a government management information system, or MIS. 

00:37 We will go through why we need to clean data, removing blank rows from the data, using the clear option in Excel, filling in blank cells, and finally, we'll look at how to set up macros to do this repetitive task of data cleaning. 

00:54 We'll start by describing a hypothetical situation that you're likely to experience in the government context in India and then we'll go about discussing the skills we would need to address it. Although we're using an example from a particular scheme, the skills we will discuss can be generalized. So let's imagine you work for an office which is involved with the monitoring and management of roads that are constructed under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana or PMGSY scheme. You use the data from the scheme's national MIS to conduct your data analysis. So you have to download and clean the data in order to begin your analysis.

01:32 The MIS data downloaded in an Excel sheet looks like this:

01:33 Most government MIS systems have the option to download the data in an Excel format. And if not, then people usually copy and paste the data into an Excel sheet in order to do the analysis. Unfortunately, due to the peculiarities of the way that the data is displayed on the MIS, the downloaded data often looks like this and it's not immediately ready for analysis. 

01:58 Look at the data downloaded from the MIS:

01:59 The downloaded data may have hidden or merged cells like you can see here, in the boxes outlined in red. In this format, it'll be hard to immediately apply the formulas to the entire rows or columns or to create pivot tables as you will most likely run into errors. So we will need to clean up this data in order to make it ready for analysis. 

02:23 Why should you clean your data?

02:24 We know it's important to clean the data before you begin your analysis. So let's discuss why we need to clean the data. By cleaning it, we can keep it in a standard structured format that is easy to both store and share. It makes it easier to extract and analyze the data, not just in Excel but also through any other programs or languages that you may need to use. And it also reduces the chances of errors during analysis. If you're interested in learning more about data cleaning and how to best arrange and store your data, I would suggest reading about tidy data and some links for this are shared at the end in the resources section. The three basic principles of tidy data are 1. That each variable forms a column, 2. Each observation forms a row, and 3. Each value must have its own cell. 

03:12 In the following slides, we will not be implementing all the principles of tidy data, but we will be addressing the key concerns that we face when we download data from an MIS. So we will be looking at cleaning the formatting, filling in blank cells after unmerging cells, and then how to set up a macro so that we can save time and don't have to do this task of data cleaning again and again.

03:38 Create a copy of your data

03:38 We will first start by creating a copy of your data. We do this to prevent the loss of data and it's generally a great practice to have backups and it would also help in case we make any errors so that we can always go back to the original data instead of replicating and making decisions based on bad data. 

03:58 Clear formatting

03:59 The second step we will be doing is to clear the formatting. Excel has a built-in clear option and you will see where to find it when we look at the screen recording. Once you click clear, like you can see in the screenshot on the right, you will see a drop-down. And we will use the clear formats option that that you can see there. Using this option will clear all the formatting such as any conditional formatting that has been applied or number formatting, or things like fonts, colors, borders, etc., that may have been added to your data. 

04:29 Removing blank rows

04:30 Next, we'll remove the blank rows. Like with the general reasons that I discussed for why we should clean our data, it's the same with the blank rows. These can interfere with our analysis, so it's better to remove them before we start. In this case, we have a small data set, so we can easily just manually delete the blank rows and columns. And in the data that we download from an MIS, such blank rows and columns usually occur at the extremes, like at the top or bottom or extreme left or right. But if the data set is very large, then you can use the find and select option in Excel that we will discuss later to be able to remove the blank rows more easily. 

05:12 Easy hack to fill blanks

05:13 Next, we'll go through an easy hack to fill in the blank cells that will come up once we clear the formatting and remove the merged cells. The first step will be to select the blank cells. Now we can't select all of them together the way that we usually select cells because they're dispersed here and there. So we'll be using the find and select option in Excel and you'll see how to use this when I show you the screen recording. 

05:44 Easy hack to fill blanks

05:45 After you use find and select, all the blank cells will get selected. Now think back to the original data that we downloaded. Why were these cells merged in the first place? This was because the values were the same. So whoever created the data format thought it would look cleaner if all the cells with the same values were merged. And usually, when cells are merged, the value in the top or leftmost cell is applied to the merged cells. So now we know how to figure out what the missing value in the blank cell should be.

06:19 Easy hack to fill blanks

06:20 To enter the value from the above cell into the blank cells, we'll use this easy hack where we will enter equal to and then press the up arrow. You'll see how we do this when I show you the screen recording. And then we'll press control and enter together to apply it. The value above it will get entered, but it will be as a reference to a cell above. Now this can be messy when we analyze data, so we will address it by using the space paste special option to just paste in the correct values. 

06:55 Let's see the steps to follow...

06:55 Now that we've discussed all the steps, let's go through the screen recording to see how to apply them in Excel.

07:03 Some commonly used keyboard shortcuts:

07:04 We'll be using these common keyboard shortcuts to select, open a new sheet, copy and paste our data.

997.lesson_title: Mail Merge in Microsoft Word and Excel
997.text:
This is the Public Sector Data Science Course, where we teach data-related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

In this module, we'll be focusing on one particular function offered in Microsoft Word. We learn the basics of Mail Merge, how to prepare the Excel data to use with Mail Merge, and finally, how to save and print the personalized documents. 

We'll start by describing a hypothetical situation that you're likely to experience in the government context in India and then we'll go about discussing the skills we would need to address it. Although we're using an example from a particular scheme, the skills that we'll discuss are generalizable. In this case, your reporting officer has asked you to prepare a D.O. letter to be sent to the Chief Secretary of every state. The aim of the letter is to tell them to take notice of their state's performance in PMGSY and review it. Beyond the context of a government letter and specifically a D.O. letter, you can use Mail Merge in a variety of different contexts.

So what is Mail Merge? Mail Merge is a feature in Microsoft Word that lets you create personalized/customized text within a set format. It can be used in letters, e-mails, labels, or any other type of text-based output and Mail Merge can help you do this entire process faster.

The concept of the D.O. letter mentioned in the exercise may be new to some of you, so let me first explain what I meant by a D.O. letter. D.O. means a demiofficial letter, and these are used in the government to communicate a little more casually than with an official letter. It can be used to share updates, invite suggestions and comments, and also include detailed facts and figures. Like I'd said earlier, this is just one case where Mail Merge can be used. It can otherwise be used in any context where you need to integrate information stored in an Excel into a document or an e-mail. 

So let's go over some tips to write an effective D.O. letter. You should start with being clear about the objective of the letter you're writing, provide the context and include state-specific information, have a clear ask or call to action in the letter, convey the level of urgency with which you're writing, if it's very urgent or something that they can take a time a little time with, and overall your letter should be clear, short, and to the point.

So let's look at the sample letter I have prepared and see the places where we can apply Mail Merge. So this is the body of the letter with the details. We have the end with the address where the copies have to be sent, and later the appendix with the relevant data for that state. Now let's start from the beginning and see all the fields that can be automatically customized or personalized for each state. So at the very top, there's the name of the officer, then the state's name, then state-specific data, like all of these details for the roads that you can see and their performance. Then the address where the letter has to be sent, again the state's name, and then finally in the appendix, the state's name and then all the state-specific data. 

So here are all the places that we had marked out in the letter where we can use Mail Merge. And at the bottom highlighted in red, I have put the Excel columns that we would use to fill in all these places. So things like the state name, the target length of the road, the completed length, the percentage completed that you can see in the box in the top, and then for the address, the name and designation of the officer, the address, the city and district that they're in and then the pin code. And all of these details will also then plug into the table in the appendix.

Before you start using Mail Merge, you have to make sure that your Excel sheet that you have to use is ready. And it's the easiest for you to use if all the data that you need is in one sheet, rather than on multiple sheets. So one tip is to use column header names that are easy to understand and format the data in the columns keeping in mind how you would want it to show in the text of the letter. You should be careful when formatting data especially as percentages, because when it gets integrated into Word, it'll appear as a decimal value. So it's better to multiply it by 100 so that it shows exactly how you would want it to in the letter and we'll go over more tips on formatting numbers later in this module. Now let's look at the Excel sheet that we'll be using and get started on actually implementing Mail Merge.

So this is the Excel sheet we'll be using and here you can see how all the scheme-related data has been put together and the names of the columns that we'll be using. So these data sets are usually separate, the scheme data and the addresses, but we've put them all together into one sheet to make it easy. Now to start with Mail Merge, go to the mailings tab. See the start Mail Merge option, go to select recipients and say choose from existing list, select the Excel sheet with your data and press open. In this, select sheet one and tick the option saying first row of data contains column headers and click OK. Now Mail Merge will start to be implemented because you've linked the Excel sheet with all of your data.

So let's see how now that the Excel data has been linked, how can we start to integrate this information and start automating how the letter gets personalized. So if you remember how we'd gone about highlighting the data in the letter that we had made, the first thing that we highlighted as a place to use Mail Merge was the greeting line where you can see I added it on the top where it says Dear Shri. Kumar Sanjay Krishna. So this is where you have the salutation and the officer's name, and because we're sending this letter to every state, the name of the officer should change as per the state where it's being sent. So we'll see how we can personalize this using Mail Merge and I'll show you a screen recording that has all the steps.

So in the Word document first, highlight the greeting line, then click the greeting line option in the Mail Merge tab. The insert Mail Merge box will appear, and you can see the preset options that Excel already has in the dropdown menus, and as you select them, you can see the preview below for how it will appear. So if it's not showing up in the format that you want, you can go to the match fields option below, and then you can use this match field box to format the greeting line as per your requirements. So here we can match it so in our case, all of the information is together in one column, the entire name of the officer. As you can see here, the whole name, the salutation, the name, the middle name and the last name are all in one column and not in separate columns. So we'll have to change the format that Excel has preset. So we can just select our data, our column header which said name, which had all the information as part of the first name dropdown, and click OK. So now you can see that it's actually appearing in the format that we wanted, so we'll click OK. So now you can see that because the greeting line Mail Merge has been implemented, where the greeting line used to be, now this greeting line message has appeared to say that the greeting line Mail Merge has been applied.

Now let's try the Address Block because there are many different fields here, which will have to be customized to implement the Mail Merge for the Address Block and just like with the greeting line Mail Merge, Excel has a preset option for the Address Block, and like with the greeting line, in case one of these preset options does not meet your requirement, you can again use the match fields option to customize it so that it appears exactly how you would want it to. So let's see the screen recording to see how we would go about doing this.

So like before we'll select the address text and click Address Block in the options and this box will open. So we'll go down to match fields, and change the dropdowns to make sure that it matches exactly what we want. So here you could see that where it said company, I have chosen designation, so I'll explain why exactly we did that, but you can see it matches the format that we want, and once we clicked OK, the address text has been replaced with this thing, Address Block, which means that the merge has been implemented.

So I'm just showing that step again where I had used the designation in place of the company name, so that the designation which is Chief Secretary appears right after the officer's name, as you can see in the preview on the right where we have first the officer's name, Shri. Kumar Sanjay Krishna, followed by their designation, which is Chief Secretary and then the address and the rest of the details. So if you want to add this designation after the person's name, or the name of the department or anything like that, you can check the insert company option in the address of block box that appears, so you can see it's been highlighted in the red rectangle with the arrow. So we'll check off that option that says insert company name in the first screen, and then when we go into match fields, when the company name option appears, you can select designation, so it'll appear like this. So this is one of the hacks I used to make sure the address block appears exactly in the format that I want.

So once the merge has been implemented, it will look like this. Now let's go back to the letter that we had marked out for Mail Merge and you can see that we've put in the merge for the greeting line, where I put the first a black check mark, and then the address block at the bottom. But we have all of the other places that are highlighted in yellow remaining. So in the following sections of this module, we'll learn how to insert the merge fields for the remaining highlighted sections.

So all of the remaining fields, which are state name, target construction, the length of the road that's already been constructed, percentage constructed and all of the data that's in the appendix table, all of this can be merged using the insert merge field option that's there in Excel. And I'll show you exactly how to use it. So this is the insert Mail Merge field option and as soon as you click it, you will get all of the options, the dropdown showing all of the column headers from Excel and you can select your data source and that will get inserted as the merge field. So let's see in the screen recording how you'll go about doing this.

So first we can select the state name, we'll highlight it, click insert merge field and click state. And you can see it's immediately been replaced, so then we can go down and do the same for the rest of the fields that have to be merged. So again the state's name appears, so we'll follow the same steps, highlight it, insert merge field, select state, then with the rest of the data. And the target roads, we'll highlight it, go to insert merge field, select target length, similarly for the rest of the places. Length completed, percentage of the length completed, then again wherever the state's name appears again at the bottom, so again we'll select state and then we'll follow the same procedure for all of the steps in the appendix as well.

So we'll repeat all again the same steps where we'll highlight the name or the data point, select insert merge field, and select the name of the column header that's there in Excel and once we've done all of that, this is what the an extra table will look like. So all of these fields, all of the data points have now been merged and will directly draw the data from your Excel table. You can use this highlight merge fields option to see exactly where it's been inserted and then you can preview results to look at how the letter will look like once the fields have been merged. So I'll show you the screen recording how you'll go about doing this.

So we highlight Merge Fields, so all of the merge fields will get highlighted in the entire letter, here you can see the merge fields have been highlighted and then if we click preview results, you can see how the letter will look like once the fields have been merged. So this is for Andaman, so that officer's name, then if you click next, Arunachal, Assam, Bihar, all of these states, their personalized letters will appear with the name of their officer and the state-specific data. Now as we're going through the previews, you can obviously see some things that aren't looking very right, like how you can see in this letter for Kerala, if you look at the second paragraph of the letter where we're showing the percentage of the road that's been completed, look at the number of decimal points that are showing there. 5.63366666666. Now this is in exactly how we should be formatting the numbers for a letter. 

Look at the number of decimal places shown here. This is the example from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands letter. So, now there's one problem with Mail Merge that we're highlighting by showing you this. So when you apply the Mail Merge, it doesn't exactly adhere to the number format that's there in Excel. In Excel, we just had two decimal places or three decimal places, but you can see here that it's not following that same format. So by looking at this, it's important to remember that any numeric values, percentages, dates, currencies or any other numbers that you use in Mail Merge will not likely retain their formatting once they're inserted into Microsoft Word.

So if we want to fix this, we have to edit the field code. So actually behind each of the merge fields that we've applied, there's a field code that decides its formatting and these field codes can be altered to design and decide exactly how the field should appear, what results should appear when it's integrated into Microsoft Word. So in this case, we want to alter the number of decimal places that appears for each of those numbers and we want it to say be like two decimal places.

So I'll show you in the screen recording how you can go about editing the field codes. So you highlight the merge field and right click and say toggle field code and edit it with a forward slash, then hash, and then I'm writing 0.00 because I want my number to appear with two decimal places, and we'll follow the same process for all of the other fields that have to be merged, forward slash, hash, 0.00 again because we want two decimal places, and by following this process, you alter the field code below, and then you say update field code for it to get applied. Once you've said update field code, it actually saves the changes that you've made. 

So let's go over exactly what we did to edit the field code. So first we selected the merge field, right clicked and selected the toggle field code option, and then it appeared like this with a brackets merge field, and then to that we edited it by leaving a space after the field name and then typing forward slash, forward slash, hash, again a space, 0.00 for two decimal places, and say you wanted three decimal places then you would write 0.000. So the number of zeros that you put in after the decimal place will decide exactly how the formatting will appear. And once you've made these changes, you again right click and select update field to save your changes and then again you can preview the merge to see exactly how it appears and check whether the formatting has been updated correctly.

So you can follow the same steps as we'd followed earlier to update the field codes for all of the data in the appendix table below. And you can also add in symbols such as currency signs or the percentage symbols or any other thing that you want to make the formatting exactly how you want them to. So now that we've fixed all the merge fields, let's see how we can complete the merge and then print them or save them as individual documents. 

Let's see how to preview the results and then finally edit the recipient list that will help us decide which all state's letters will get created. So if you click the edit recipient list, this kind of box will open that will show you all of the fields that you have personalized for each state. So I'll just start by unchecking it so that I can review the data and then decide finally which all state's letters I want to be created. So here I can see that the data for Goa is incomplete as I scroll through the table and so I decide to not check that box as I don't want an incomplete letter to be created. Similarly you can go down and keep checking the data for all the different states. Again, Ladakh has some incomplete fields so I don't want that letter to be created. Alternatively, you can also create the letter and then edit it later. So it's up to you to decide how you want the letters to be created. So I've selected all of them and clicked OK. Now I can go and preview all of the letters for which I had selected the recipients. So because I hadn't selected Goa, a preview isn't created for it. Then you can end by clicking Finish and Merge. You can either print all the documents or you can select edit individual documents. You can decide whether you want all of them or the current one and whatever you select to edit individually will open as a separate Word document. So here the Jharkhand letter has opened as its own document. And using these two steps, either to open it separately as a word document or to print it, you can bring your process of creating a letter with Mail Merge to an end, and deciding how you want to use it finally.

So let's go over some things that we've already covered in this module. So the first is if you draft your letter in advance, and if you're clear about the exact content that you'll be using, it will make your entire process much easier and it will make it much faster to finalize. Also, the Excel sheet that you need and how you need to break up your data in the Excel sheet, whether you want the name all together, whether you want the first and last name separately, how you want to spread up the address information and things like that. The third thing is using the match fields option when you're using the preset merge options that are there in Excel in in Word, like greeting line and address block. You saw how we had to go into the match fields to customize them to make them fit exactly the format that we wanted. This is the Public Sector Data Science course where we teach data related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

In this session, we'll be going over the basics of descriptive statistics in the context of government scheme data. We'll go over an introduction to descriptive stats, then look at how to create five-number summaries, then how to use the analysis ToolPak in Excel, and finally end with a discussion on interpreting and comparing descriptive statistics. 

We'll start by describing a hypothetical situation that you are likely to experience in the government context and then we'll go about discussing the skills we would need to address it. Although we're using an example from a particular scheme, the skills that we will discuss can be generalized. In this case, imagine that you work on the Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana or DDUGKY and you need to understand the trends in the salaries received by candidates who have been placed into jobs through the program. 

Based on the problem statement, we can use descriptive statistics to understand the distribution of salaries of people placed into jobs after receiving training through DDUGKY? 

So what are descriptive statistics? These types of statistics help us summarize and understand patterns in the data and include things like frequency, central tendency, and dispersion of the data. Using such analysis can help us to look at patterns in the data and potentially come up with actionable insights.

The data we will be using today as an example for this analysis contains individual-level data for candidates placed after DDUGKY training and it tells you the district name, as you can see in column A on the left, district_name, the candidate's unique ID, which is the column named unique_candidateid, the designation, the sector, which is the column D named sector_name, and the trade name for the position that they've been placed in, and the salary, which is the last column, column F. And there are more than 40,000 rows of data in the set that we'll be using to go through this example. 

In the government context, we often default to using the average or mean as our go-to measure of central tendency to start our analysis. However, there are many challenges with doing this.

Look at the graph shown here. This is just an example to discuss the pitfalls of averages. The graph shows the salaries of students employed in the IT sector after graduation. So on the Y-axis, you have the number of students, and on the X-axis, you have their salaries. So in this case, what do you think will be larger, the median or the mean? 

In this case, the mean will be larger due to the extreme values that you can see on the right side of the axis. So in this case, the mean is not a good measure of central tendencies for salaries in the IT sector and we should be using the median instead. These are the kinds of factors that we should consider when deciding whether to use a median or the mean when we're looking at our data and want to find a measure of central tendency. 

The first analysis for descriptive statistics that we'll go through in this session is how to calculate a five-number summary for your data because it's a good starting point. A five-number summary consists of five values. The most extreme value in the data set, which is both the maximum, which is the highest value, and the minimum, which is the lowest value, it also includes the lower and upper quartiles and the median. These values are represented together and from the lowest to the highest, they are shown minimum value, then the lower quartile, which is Q1, then the median value, Q2, the upper quartile, Q3, and the maximum value. These values have been selected to form the five-number summary because they give a good representation of the data set that you're working with. 

So this is a visual representation of the five-number summary. If you start walking from one end like the little figure shown here on the left, where you are standing and starting from will be the minimum value. This is if the numbers are arranged in ascending order from the smallest to the largest. By the time you reach Q1, you would have crossed 25% of the values and 25% of the path that you have to walk, which will be your entire data set. The median represents the central point, so on either side you'll have equal distance to keep walking. By the time you reach Q3, you would have walked 75% of the way, and the maximum value will be the very last point when you're walking on this journey. I hope this helps to give you an understanding of what the different numbers in the five-number summary represent if you're looking at your data set as a whole. 

So now I'll show you two methods to calculate these descriptive statistics in Excel. The first is by using basic Excel functions and formulas, and the second is by using an Excel analysis ToolPak add-in option. 

Let's get started with looking at the first method using basic Excel functions. 

These are the Excel formulas we'll use to calculate the five-number summary for the salary data for DDUGKY. Like I had shared earlier, as the name suggests, the five-number summary consists of five values, the minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and the maximum. Excel has formulas for all of these which I have written here and they are quite straightforward to use. For the minimum value, we use the MIN function in Excel. For this, we have to select the entire range of numbers which we want to take the minimum value for. Then we have the Q1 value, which is calculated using the quartile function in Excel. For this, first you select the range of the numbers for which you need to calculate the first quartile value, and then you enter 1, 2, or 3, depending on which quartile you want to get the value for. Like with the minimum, you can use the built-in maximum function and select the entire range for which you want to find the maximum value, close the bracket, and press enter. You can also use Excel's quartile function to calculate the minimum and maximum values. If you're using the quartile function, the minimum will be quartile 0, so you'll select the range, press comma, and enter 0 before you close the bracket, and the maximum will be quartile 4, so similarly you can type the quartile function, open the bracket, select the range, comma, and enter 4 to close the bracket, press enter, and get the maximum value. So, although I've shown you four different functions, minimum, quartile, median, and maximum, you can actually just use the quartile function to calculate all of these. (00:10) In this session, we'll be learning about histograms in Excel. We'll start with an introduction to histograms, then learn how to make them in Excel 2016 and go on to learning how to decide bins and make intervals. Then we'll make histograms using column charts, which is helpful for Excel versions prior to 2016, and end with some things to keep in mind while making histograms.

(00:38) A histogram is the most commonly used chart to visualize distribution of data. When you want to look at distribution, you want to see the frequency, how data is spread out, how it is grouped, where there are gaps, and where there are extreme values. To look at such things, you can use a histogram to visualize data over a continuous interval or time period. The heights of the bars in a histogram represent the frequency of that particular interval or bin. We can use a histogram to understand things such as data over time, patterns of data, spread of data, range, and compare distributions of data, as well as find significant outliers.

(01:22) Although column/bar charts and histograms look similar, they function differently. In column charts, each column represents a group defined by a categorical variable. In histograms, each column represents a group defined by a continuous, quantitative variable. But all versions of Excel do not have the option to automatically generate histograms. So in those cases, we can use the column chart option to make a histogram, and we'll discuss this in detail going forward.

(01:52) In the example we will look at today, we will use data from the National Rural Livelihoods Mission or NRLM. We look at the time taken to release Revolving Fund to self-help groups after their bank account has been opened. You can find other such cases in data from other schemes where there are continuous variables that can be visualized using histograms. Anywhere that there is time taken, number of days, amounts, weights, etc. For example, think of the number of NREGA person-days completed by all the households in a particular district. Here the highest number will be fixed, depending on the number of person-days permitted in the state or beneficiary type, but we can use a histogram to look at the distribution. And I'm sure you can think of other such examples from whichever government schemes you are working with.

(02:42) Excel 2016 has the option to just select data and add a histogram. Later we'll also see how histograms can be made in older versions of Excel. 

(02:55) So for Excel 2016, all you have to do is select the data, go to the histogram option in the Insert tab, and as soon as you click it, a histogram will automatically get created.

(03:25) The height of the bars in a histogram is determined by the count of the observations falling into each bin/interval. Thus the size of the bins is an important parameter in a histogram. The choice of bin size can obscure or distort the underlying data. Changing the bin width can change the number of observations falling into that bin and affect the shape of the distribution that you see. However, there is no standard rule on deciding the bin size, and you can decide the bin size depending on what makes sense for your data and how you can justify it.
