When you want to look at distribution, you want to see the frequency, how data is spread out, how it is grouped, where there are gaps, and where there are extreme values. To look at such things, you can use a histogram to visualize data over a continuous interval or time period. The heights of the bars in a histogram represent the frequency of that particular interval or bin. We can use a histogram to understand things such as data over time, patterns of data, spread of data, range, and compare distributions of data, as well as find significant outliers.

(01:22) Although column/bar charts and histograms look similar, they function differently. In column charts, each column represents a group defined by a categorical variable. In histograms, each column represents a group defined by a continuous, quantitative variable. But all versions of Excel do not have the option to automatically generate histograms. So in those cases, we can use the column chart option to make a histogram, and we'll discuss this in detail going forward. (01:52) In the example we will look at today, we will use data from the National Rural Livelihoods Mission or NRLM. We look at the time taken to release Revolving Fund to self-help groups after their bank account has been opened. You can find other such cases in data from other schemes where there are continuous variables that can be visualized using histograms. Anywhere that there is time taken, number of days, amounts, weights, etc. For example, think of the number of NREGA person-days completed by all the households in a particular district.

For example, think of the number of NREGA person-days completed by all the households in a particular district. Here the highest number will be fixed, depending on the number of person-days permitted in the state or beneficiary type, but we can use a histogram to look at the distribution. And I'm sure you can think of other such examples from whichever government schemes you are working with. (02:42) Excel 2016 has the option to just select data and add a histogram. Later we'll also see how histograms can be made in older versions of Excel. (02:55) So for Excel 2016, all you have to do is select the data, go to the histogram option in the Insert tab, and as soon as you click it, a histogram will automatically get created. (03:08) This is what the auto-generated histogram looks like, but unfortunately it doesn't help us much. To understand why it looks like this, we need to understand the size of the bins or the intervals used. (03:25) The height of the bars in a histogram is determined by the count of the observations falling into each bin/interval. Thus the size of the bins is an important parameter in a histogram.

Thus the size of the bins is an important parameter in a histogram. The choice of bin size can obscure or distort the underlying data. Changing the bin width can change the number of observations falling into that bin and affect the shape of the distribution that you see. However, there is no standard rule on deciding the bin size, and you can decide the bin size depending on what makes sense for your data and how you can justify it. (04:05) Since we are showing the number of days taken for RF release after the SHG has opened its bank account, let's see what we know about RF and the relevance of time taken. Similarly, if you are making a histogram for other scheme data, try to look at how the data links to the processes to be followed in the scheme. For this you can look at the scheme guidelines and other such relevant documents. In the guidelines for NRLM, ideally, the SHG should have a savings bank account three months after formation, and the RF should be received by the SHG between three to four months after SHG formation. So in this case, maybe we can take the first bin size to be less than four months, or less than 120 days.

So in this case, maybe we can take the first bin size to be less than four months, or less than 120 days. Since this is different from the bins that have been auto-created by Excel, we will have to set the custom bin sizes ourselves. (05:10) Apart from setting the custom bin width at 120, we will also be setting the underflow and overflow bins. Underflow bin: we will set this at 120. So all the observations under 120 will fall into this. This will show us how many SHGs received the RF within 120 days or 4 months of account opening. Overflow bin: we will set this at 1320. So all the observations over 1320 will go into this. This will show us how many SHGs received the RF more than 1320 days or 44 months after their account opening. (05:55) Double-click on the x-axis and the formatting pane on the right should open. Go to axis options and select bin width. Set the bin width at 120 as we had discussed and you can see how the histogram changes. Then go back to the formatting pane by double-clicking and set the underflow bin at 120 and the overflow bin at 1320. Again, you can see how the histogram changes.

Again, you can see how the histogram changes. Close the formatting pane, select the gridlines and delete them, and you can also delete the data labels for the y-axis. You can change the size of the chart to make it more legible. (06:54) The final histogram will appear like this. To improve the formatting of the chart, we removed the y-axis labels because they were adding extra clutter and the number of SHGs is clear from the data labels. The x-axis labels are not very clear and intuitive to read, but there is no option to change these in the histogram chart in Excel 2016. This can be changed by creating a column chart as a histogram and we'll discuss this as we go on further in this session. (07:30) The option to automatically create histograms is not available in older versions of Excel, so we can make the chart using a frequency table and a Column chart. The first step will be to create the bins or intervals and grouping the data into those through a frequency distribution. (07:53) First we'll create a table like the one shown below with the brackets you want to use. Then we will use the FREQUENCY function in Excel to see how many SHGs fall into each bin.

Then we will use the FREQUENCY function in Excel to see how many SHGs fall into each bin. The numbers in the first column will be the upper limit of each bin, and the second column will be the data labels that we want to show on the chart. We will use the frequency function in Excel to see how many SHGs fall into each bin, and we'll use that to fill the third column. (08:16) This is the frequency function that we'll be using. The function has two parts: the data array, the first part will be the list of all observations. In our case, the whole list of days taken for RF dispersal for each SHG. And the bins array, the second part will be from the first row in the frequency table that we just saw. This will form the upper limit of the data. In Excel versions prior to 2013, you have to press the Control key along with the Shift and Enter keys to implement this function properly. Now let's see how we'll use this function to fill the table. (08:58) Select the third row where you want the frequencies to appear. Type in "=FREQUENCY" and open the bracket and then select the entire data array. Then enter comma and select the bins array.

Type in "=FREQUENCY" and open the bracket and then select the entire data array. Then enter comma and select the bins array. Close the bracket and press Ctrl+Shift+Enter and the frequencies will get filled. (09:25) Now that we have the numbers in the frequency table, we have to make a histogram on the right using the column chart option. (10:05) The first step is simple, select the frequency table and insert a column chart. (10:17) This is the column chart we just created. Now we have to format it to look like a histogram. The main thing to make it look like a histogram is to reduce the gap between the columns. Then we can add data labels to the columns and we can also remove the y-axis labels as we did in the automatic histogram and add a title for the x-axis below. (10:45) Click on the columns and go to the Series Option in the formatting pane. There reduce the gap width to as little as possible. Here I've reduced it to 2%. Then add data labels to the columns. You can delete the ones for the y-axis and add axis titles. For the y-axis, we can type in "Number of SHGs" and for the x-axis, we can type in "Number of days between account opening and RF dispersal".

For the y-axis, we can type in "Number of SHGs" and for the x-axis, we can type in "Number of days between account opening and RF dispersal". (11:38) This will be the histogram after formatting. Although it takes more time to make than the automatic histogram, this may be a better option even for those using Excel 2016 onwards as you have control over what the x-axis labels look like and can make them clearer. (12:00) This brings us to the end of this module on histograms. So let's go over some limitations and things to keep in mind. The first is that histograms can only be used with continuous data. The second is that you lose out on granularity in some sense when you make a histogram as you don't see each individual observation. And because of this grouping, you can't tell the measures of central tendency like the average or median number of days taken. And because of the underflow and overflow bins we have used in this case, we cannot tell the exact maximum or minimum values. The most important thing to keep in mind while making histograms is that the display and insights are very dependent on the bin size and can distort the data.

Once you keep this in mind, you can realize the benefits of using histograms. Histograms can be not just a tool for communication but also to explore the data and understand it better and see gaps or trends that you may not see otherwise. It can help to highlight issues and areas where action is needed, and it can be more compelling than putting it in a table or writing the insights in a textual form. But again and again, I will also emphasize that the visualization can also hide as much as it can reveal. You can think back to what we discussed in the other module on descriptive statistics, where the data looks very different but has all the same summary statistics. I'd encourage you to go back and re-watch that module. What you see in the data visualization is shaped by the assumptions and decisions you make while creating the visualization and it's important to keep that in mind. (13:38) As always, here is a resource that you can use when you get started with making your own histograms.

1002.text:
Welcome to the Public Sector Data Science Course where we teach data-related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

In this presentation we will look at comparison of data using scatter plots and then I will introduce you to a free online tool called RawGraphs. For this module we will be using data from the National Rural Livelihoods Mission or NRLM to go through different examples of data visualizations. As always, the learnings can be applied across different contexts and are not limited to NRLM. 

Looking at comparisons between data
- As per the NRLM guidelines, the households listed in SECC can act as a reference point for the identification of poor households for inclusion in SHGs.
- So one way to see saturation of the scheme would be to look at the number of households that meet auto-inclusion and at least one of the SECC criteria for deprivation, and then compare that with the SHG data.
- SECC data is available at the household level and for SHGs we have the number of SHG members. Since one household usually has one SHG member, we can take number of SHG members to be a proxy for the number of households with an SHG member.

Since we are using data from the National Rural Livelihoods Mission or NRLM for this module, let's discuss how we can look at comparison of different government data sets to draw insights about a scheme. And this can be done beyond NRLM and with other schemes as well. Apart from NRLM data, here we'll also be talking about data from the SECC or Socio-Economic and Caste Census, which was last conducted in 2011. This data set has a lot of details that we can use to understand the nature of households that should be included in schemes, and what kind of services they should be able to access. To know more about how SECC data can be used, I would suggest going to the SECC website and reading more about it and also exploring what the data means in the context of your area of work. Now let's come back to discussing SECC in the context of NRLM and how we can compare data to draw insights. 

As per the NRLM guidelines, the households listed in SECC can act as a reference point for the identification of poor households for inclusion in SHGs or self-help groups. 
So one way to see saturation of the NRLM scheme would be to look at the number of households that meet auto-inclusion and at least one of the SECC criteria for deprivation and then compare that with SHG data. Again, here if you are unfamiliar with the terms auto-inclusion and deprivation criteria, I would recommend that you try to read more about both SECC and inclusion criteria used by your program. The SECC data is available at the household level and for SHGs, we have the number of SHG members. Since one household usually has one SHG member and this is an assumption that we're making based on data available, we can take the number of SHG members to be a proxy for the number of households with an SHG member. Before we go on to actually doing this comparison of data to look at the scheme saturation, it's important for us to note that often, when we use different data sets for comparison, they don't match exactly. So we may end up making assumptions like we did in this case. And if you do make assumptions, it's important to note them and include these assumptions whenever you present your data or use it for any report or decision making so that your analysis is not misleading and your audience is clear about the assumptions you're making and how they should account for them when they look at your data. 

- Using a scatter plot, we can compare the number of SHG members to the number of households meeting auto-inclusion or at least one criteria for deprivation to look at SHG saturation.
- Other examples where we can look at comparisons of data:
    - For NREGA, comparison between SC/ST active workers and payment delays
    - For PMAY-G, comparison between NREGA persondays/employment and PMAY-G household coverage

In this case we're going to visualize our comparison of data by using a scatter plot. By using a scatter plot we can compare the number of SHG members to the number of households meeting auto-inclusion or at least one criteria for deprivation through the SECC data to look at SHG saturation. Other examples where we can look at comparisons of data to draw insights are for example NREGA, where we can look at the comparison between SC and ST active workers and their related payment delays. And for example, we can look at PMAY-G where we can see the comparison between NREGA person days or employment and PMAY-G household coverage to make inferences about the implementation of the scheme. 

What is a scatter plot?
A scatter plot uses dots on a chart to represent 2 different numerical values.
The dot is placed at the intersection of the 2 values, one placed on the x-axis and the other on the y-axis.
The scatter plot is used to examine the relationship between the two sets of numerical values mapped by the dots.
In a scatter plot, we can gain insight from the position of each individual dot as well as from the pattern formed by the distribution of all the dots seen together.

So what is a scatter plot? Before we go into making them, let's look at what they are all about. A scatter plot uses dots on a chart to represent 2 different numerical values. These are from the two different data sets that we're comparing or two different items, or whatever it is, categories that we may be comparing. The dot is placed at the intersection of the two values, one value which is on the x-axis and the other which is on the y-axis. The scatter plot is used to examine the relationship between the two sets of numerical values that are mapped by these dots. In a scatter plot we can gain insight from the position of each individual dot, as well as from the pattern that's formed by the distribution of all of the dots seen together. 

When to use a scatter plot:
When you want to compare or see a relationship between two variables.
To identify patterns in the data - to see if the data is being grouped in certain ways or if there are particular outliers.
BUT changes in one value are not necessarily responsible for changes in the other. Correlation does not imply causation.

So when should we use a scatter plot? You can use this when you want to compare or see a relationship between two variables, exactly how we had discussed in the case of NRLM. You can use it to identify patterns in data to see if data is being grouped in certain ways or if there are particular outliers. But it's important to note that changes in one value are not necessarily responsible for changes in the other. As you may have heard many times over, it's important to see and note and keep in mind that correlation does not imply causation. 

When to not use a scatter plot:
In cases where you have too many data points, for example all the blocks from all the districts of India, then the dots will overlap and it will not be possible to identify the individual points and see the relationships between the data.
In this case, it may be better to use another type of visualisation or create the scatter using a randomly selected sample of the data.

So one way to make a quick, more visually appealing chart like a scatter plot is using your Excel data and creating the chart through a website called app.rawgraphs.io. So RawGraphs is a free and open source online tool for data visualization. 

What is RawGraphs?
It is an open source data visualisation framework with the aim of making data visualisation easy for everyone.
It can be used directly through your web browser by visiting the website linked above.
After adding your data, you can even experiment with different types of visualisations to see what works best.

So it's an open source data visualisation framework with the aim of making data visualisation easy for everyone. And RawGraphs can be used directly through your web browser by visiting the link that I had shared, and after adding your data you can also experiment with different types of visualisations. So it's not just limited to scatter plots, but I had found their way of creating scatter plots to be quite useful so I decided to integrate it with this module. But otherwise you can use RawGraphs to create any kind of data visualization with different types of data. So let's see a screen recording of how you can use the data that we already had in Excel and put it onto RawGraphs online tool and create a better-looking scatter plot. 

What can we learn from a scatter plot?
We can observe relationships between the data:
- strong, moderate, weak or null
- positive or negative
- linear or non-linear
We can identify: clusters/groups, gaps in the data, and outliers

Some things to keep in mind
Not every graph has data points that clearly all lie close to a straight line.
Two possibilities which may arise are:
- the underlying relationship is linear but there are outliers - they may need to be ignored or rechecked
- the underlying relationship is not linear - the line of best fit is a curve, not a straight line (non-liner)

Some things to keep in mind as we come to the end of this module is that not every graph has data points that clearly all lie close to a straight line as we just saw in the previous slide, there can be non-linear correlations, there can be a null relationship, so there are two possibilities other possibilities that may arise. The first is that the underlying relationship is linear but there are outliers that may need to be ignored or rechecked, so these are the kind of next steps that you can come up with once you finish visualizing your data in the form of a scatter plot. And the second is that the underlying relationship is not linear how we had seen in the the slide the previous slide that there was a non-linear relationship. The dots together formed a curve. So in this case, the line of best fit will be a curve and not a straight line. So this brings us to the end of this module on scatter plots and how to use them.

And as always, here is a resource that you can use when you're implementing this skill.

1004.text:
Public Sector Data Science Course. 2022.

Public Sector Data Science Course, where we teach data-related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

Principles of Effective Data Visualisation.
Introduction to Data Visualisation.
Basics of effective visualisations.
Formatting effective visualisations.

In this module, we'll be focusing on the principles of effective data visualisation. 

Primarily, we'll be looking at visualisations that are created in Excel. 

First, we'll start with a broad introduction to data visualisation, then go on to the basics of effective visualisations, and end with some formatting tips that we should keep in mind. 

WHAT IS DATA VISUALISATION?
"visually display measured quantities by means of the combined use of points, lines, a coordinate system, numbers, symbols, words and shading"
"often the most effective way to describe, explore, and summarize a set of numbers"
(source: The Visual Display of Quantitative Information by Edward Tufte)

So what is data visualisation?

Visualising data is the process by which we visually display measured quantities by using a combination of lines, points, numbers, symbols, etc.

It is often the most effective way to describe, explore and summarize a set of numbers. 

Using Data Visualisations
In the context of government schemes, you can use visualisations to ask and understand questions such as:
- What/where are the needs?
- How do we improve service delivery or scheme coverage?
- How did we perform against targets?
- What else can we try to understand?

Data visualisations are not just a tool for communication, but can also be used to explore data and understand it better.

We can see successes or gaps, trends that you may not otherwise see by looking at data in a tabular format. 

Visualisations can help to highlight issues and areas where a strategy is working or where additional action is needed. 

It can be more compelling than putting a data in a table or writing insights in a textual form. 

In our government setting, we use visualisations to ask and understand questions such as, what or where are the needs?

How do we improve service delivery or scheme coverage?

How did we perform against targets?

Or what else can we try to understand with the data that we already have in hand?

Especially because we're working in the government context, where data has deep and far-reaching implications.

It's essential to remember that the visualisations can also hide as much as they reveal. 

And what you visualise is also shaped by the assumptions and decisions that you make while creating and formatting the visualisation. 

Three basic principles to follow:
1. Show the data
2. Reduce the clutter
3. Integrate the text and graph

We'll start by looking at three principles to follow. 

The first is showing the data. 

Second is reducing the clutter and the third is integrating the text and graph. 

1. Show the data
- The data are the most important part of the graph and should be presented in the clearest way possible
- That does not mean you need to show all the data - show what is needed to communicate your objective in the best way possible
- If your data is grouped, it may be necessary to explain how or why it has been grouped in that manner.

Let's start with the first point, showing the data. 

Since the data is the most important part of the graph, it should be presented in the clearest possible way. 

But that doesn't mean that you need to put too much data into the graph. 

You need to put enough to communicate your objective. 

In case you are grouping your data, you may also need to explain why you have grouped your data in a certain way. 

2. Reduce the clutter
- The use of unnecessary or distracting visual elements, tends to reduce effectiveness of the graph.
- Clutter comes in many forms: dark or heavy gridlines; unnecessary tick marks, labels, or text; unnecessary icons or pictures; ornamental shading and gradients; and unnecessary dimensions.
- Simply put - avoid the use of 3D graphics, don't use colour gradients or shading, if you have to use grid lines then use light colours like grey.

Second is reducing the clutter. 

You should remove distracting elements that take away from the main point of your graph. 

This could be things like heavy gridlines or unnecessary graphics or text, or even things like gradients and shading in the colours that you put in your graph. 

I'd like to emphasize the point about avoiding 3D graphics and we'll come back to this later. 

And as a simple rule, you should try to avoid putting shading and textures in your graph. 

3. Integrate the text and graph
- Place supporting or explanatory information alongside the graph so that the viewer can read it alongside.
- For example, the legend should be placed right next to the graph.
- When the source of the data is not clearly indicated in your report or presentation, place information about the source/details of the data right below the graph.
- Include units of measurement where needed. Like km, rupees, lakhs etc.

Now the third point is integrating the text and graph. 

This means putting supporting information on the side, so whoever is seeing the graph can have additional information about its context. 

Like what do the colours that you've used mean, what is the source of the data and things like that. 

And include units that are useful for the data that you're using. 

Like is your data in kilometres, rupees, lakhs, etc.

Formatting effective visualisations
- Data visualisations can be made even more compelling through the way that you design and format them.
- To make your visualisations more effective, you modify things such as:
 - Colours used
 - Axes and labels
 - Legends and annotations
 - Density and clarity of information in the chart
 - Distinguishing features to highlight trends

Now let's move on to how to format visualisations to make them more compelling and effective. 

You can modify things like colours, the axes, the labels, legends, the density of the information you're sharing, as well as highlight significant data points or trends that are there in your graphs. 

In the next few slides we'll go over a series of tips that you can use to make your graphs more effective. 

Add a graph title
Use the title to give a short explanation of what is shown in your graph. This helps the reader identify what they are about to look at. It can be creative or simple as long as it tells what is in the graph.
If your audience is already familiar with the content of the graph, you can also use the title to highlight an important trend or finding from the graph. For example, “13% increase in budget allocation for FY 2022-23”.

The first thing you should keep in mind is making sure that your graph has a title. 

You can use the title to give a short introduction to what is there in your graph. 

It also depends on who your audience is. 

If the audience is familiar with the content of the graph, but immediately wants to know what's different or relevant, you can use the title to highlight a key trend or finding from your graph. 

For example, you can say, a 13% increase in budget allocation for financial year 2022-23 is what's the main finding of your graph. 

Round off numbers
Always round off numbers on the chart. If you have to use decimals for some reason, then be consistent with the number of decimal digits used across the chart. Even then, the number of decimal digits should not be more than two.

The next tip is to round off numbers. 

You should always round off numbers in your chart. 

And you can see the example on the left in red where the decimal points are shown and on the right which is with rounded off numbers. 

If you have to use decimals for some reason, then try to be consistent with the number of decimal digits you use across your chart. 

Even then, the number of decimal digits should not be more than two. 

Using more than two decimal digits in your chart takes away from the impact it's having and makes it difficult for the audience to read it. 

Intervals on the y-axis
To avoid distortion, it is better for the y-axis to start at zero.
If the y-axis intervals are automatically set, edit the intervals or bounds on the y-axis to be more meaningful and intuitive. For example, use intervals of 5, 10, 20, 100 etc instead of multiples of 2, 3, 6 etc.

The next tip is on the intervals on your y-axis. 

To avoid distortion, it is better for the y-axis to start at zero. 

If the y-axis intervals are automatically set in Excel and this often happens when you create a graph in Excel, you can edit the intervals or bounds on the y-axis to be more meaningful and intuitive for your audience. 

For example, you can use intervals of 5, 10, 20, 100 etc instead of multiples of 2, 3 and 6. 

And you can see the examples on the left and right to see what a difference it makes when you change your y-axis intervals. 

Sort your data
If you are showing data for states, districts, blocks etc. and want to show how they fare in comparison to each other, sort the data that you are using to make the visualisation. This way at a glance you can tell who is performing better or worse.

The next tip is on sorting your data. 

If you are showing data for states, districts, blocks etc., you want to show how they fare in comparison to each other, you should sort the data you are using to make your visualisation more effective. 

This way, at a glance you can tell who is performing better or worse. 

See the example on the left where the states are put in alphabetical order, but it's not intuitive to see which state is performing better. 

But as you can see on the example on the right, the states are not in alphabetical order on the x-axis, but by sorting from largest to smallest on the y-axis you can see that immediately, state B is performing the best and state A is performing the worst. 

This kind of sorting can help your audience to immediately draw insights from your data. 

Grid lines
Adding grid lines can add clutter to your chart. Avoid grid lines when data labelling can provide sufficient and clear information.

The next tip is on grid lines. 

Adding grid lines can add clutter to your chart. 

And you should avoid grid lines when data labelling can provide sufficient and clear information. 

Here you can see the examples on the left and right. 

On the left, adding the grid lines doesn't actually add that much and it's hard for your audience to see how the states are actually faring. 

But if you can see on the example on the right, the grid lines have been removed and instead data labels have been added. 

Here you can immediately see that the number for state A is 6, for C 15, D 21 and B 30. 

And again, you can see we've also added the previous principle that we had shared on sorting your data and so it's more intuitive for your audience to read it. 

Pie charts
If you are using a Pie Chart, keep the following in mind:
Don't use Pie charts when there are too many slices on the pie. It makes it difficult to compare and understand
If there are more than 5 slices, combine the smaller and less significant slices to create the fifth slice and label it 'Others'.
If all segments have to be represented separately, use a stacked/bar chart instead
In a pie chart, the largest segment should always be at 12'o hand and move clockwise. This is most intuitive for the reader

The next tip is about using pie charts. 

If you are using pie charts, you should keep the following in mind. 

Don't use pie charts when there are too many slices on the pie, as it makes it difficult to compare and understand the data. 

So if you look at the example on the left, it's really hard to see what the different categories are and how the data within them is distributed. 

So if there are more than 5 slices or categories in your data, you should combine the smaller and less significant slices to create a fifth slice and label it as others. 

And if all segments have to be represented separately, then perhaps using a pie chart is not the most effective form of visualisation and you can instead use a stacked or a bar chart instead. 

Now let's look at the graphic on the right. 

In a pie chart, the largest segment should always be at the 12 o'clock hand and move clockwise. 

This is the most intuitive for your reader. 

So this links back again to our point on sorting. 

The way that you sort your data within a graph can immediately impact the way that your audience perceives it. 

So you can look in the example on the right, the one in red, the data has not been sorted in a clockwise manner, whereas on the right, it has been done and you can immediately see that category A is the largest and as you move clockwise, the proportions decrease.

As information gets passed from one level to another, or from government to citizens, crucial information may get filtered out or a piece of analysis may be used out of its context.
So it is important for to provide as clear information as possible within the visualisation itself

An important point when making visualisations in the government is thinking about how you will share these visualisations both within and outside the government. 

As information gets passed from one level to another or from government to citizens, crucial information may get filtered out or a piece of analysis may be used outside of its intended context. 

So it's important to provide as clear as as possible information within the visualisation itself.

This is a public sector data science course where we teach data related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

In the second part of the module on making effective presentations, today we’ll be learning using themes and templates, diagrams and SmartArt and the basics of Canva for making presentations. 

Let's start with themes in PowerPoint. Themes are a combination of colours, fonts and backgrounds that you can apply to your slides to get a more professional visual look. Even within themes, there are options to choose from colour and texture combinations. 

Let's look at a screen recording on themes in PowerPoint. 

Follow these steps to use Themes in PowerPoint: 
Once you've started your PowerPoint presentation you can go into the design tab and the different theme options will be available on the top. 

You can experiment and play with the different theme options. 

As you can see that even once you select a theme there are different colour variations that are available and that you can experiment with. 

Like we had discussed earlier going with a simple theme can be more impactful for your presentation and make it easier for your audience to read your content. 

Once you've selected a theme, as you add new slides they will all come with the selected theme implemented. 

Here 4 different themes have been applied to the same content: 
You can apply a theme even after you have made your presentation so that all the slides get the same look. This is also a good option to use if you're copying and pasting different slides from different presentations to bring them together or different people in the team are making presentations. So once you have everything together you can apply the same theme. Applying the theme will change all the text font and colour to the same across all slides. This will also give a consistent and professional look to your slides and save you from spending time in manually changing fonts and colours. 

Now let's move on to discussing templates. A slide template is a pattern or blueprint for slides. Templates contain a theme but also have additional layouts, effects, content cues and visualisation formats. Beyond themes, templates can also help provide a narrative structure for the presentation. Now let's look at a screen recording on PowerPoint to see how you can use templates. 

Follow these steps to use a template in PowerPoint: 
If you started your presentation you can go into the file tab, select new and you'll see all of the different template options. 

All the templates have different categories that you can see on the right. 

So here I've opened the template category of infographics and you can see that PowerPoint has many in-built infographics. 

For example, here I've selected the infographic timeline as a template. 

This is one for a 5 year timeline. 

Here again is a more simple and effective template and theme combined. You can choose your colour options and click create to apply that to your presentation and as with the themes, every new slide you add will have the same theme applied. 

Theme & Template options. Slide themes and templates are also available through external websites and can be downloaded and used in PowerPoint. For example, through websites such as: https://templates.office.com/ A web search can help you to find other free template options. 

Govt of India Templates. Through the presentations.gov.in platform, you can access PowerPoint templates designed for government use. The platform also offers: icons, logos, animations, etc. Let's go on to look at a screen recording of how you can access these Government of India presentation templates, icons and logos. 

Follow these steps to use a template from presentations.gov.in: 
This is the homepage of the website and on the top you can see the different options. As you scroll below, you can see examples of the different templates, animations, logos and icons that they have available. 

These are the different template options that they have available they have a specific one for rural development and you can click on it and download it, and it has two different ratio options. 

So once you open it in PowerPoint this is what the file looks like. It has its theme applied as well as, because it's a template, it also gives you a flow of information and how your presentation should progress. Depending on what you're creating the presentation for you can decide to keep or remove different slides. 

Now this is the logos tab on the presentations.gov.in platform, and you can see that there are logos for different government programs, initiatives, companies and departments. 

So this is one for the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana and there are different formats in which you can download it. 

So here I've downloaded and opened the PMGSY logo and you can also get them in different size options small, medium and large. 

Edit/customise templates. You can edit a template to adapt it for your particular use case. For example: - choose the colours relevant to your department or scheme - insert your logo on every slide - add slide numbers, etc. This is done through the Slide Master option in PowerPoint. 

Let's now go on to see how we can edit the template that we downloaded just now from the presentation government website. By editing it we want to add in the PMGSY logo that we also just downloaded and also change the colours and fonts used. Now let's look at a screen recording to see how to do this on PowerPoint through the slide master option. 

Follow these steps to edit a template in PowerPoint: 
Go to the view option and then go to slide master. Here you'll see the different options of the slide master. So first we want to insert the logo that we had downloaded. So we'll do that using the insert option and resize it. And then I want to place it on the bottom left so we'll drag it there and I want to change the text that's already there in the slide master so I'll edit it to say PMGSY-III because that's what I want and the Ministry of Rural Development logo is already there on the top. I also want to change the font colour and font styles, so you can do that here and it will reflect in all the slide formats once you have edited it here in the master as you can see the text colour has changed. So wherever you see that you need to make any further changes you can do so when you're in the slide master option like I'm doing here. 

Here you can see that they've created some of the infographics so you can also change the colours for that. So that whenever you use the infographic, the colours will be what you have selected. So after you've done editing you can close the slide master view and here you can see that in the slideshow itself the changes have been implemented. The PMGSY logo is there in the bottom left, the text colours have all changed. So like this you can understand the impact that making edits in the slide master has on the template that you've downloaded or used directly from PowerPoint and how it will impact the PowerPoint presentation that you're creating. 

Edit/customise templates. - Edit your slide master and layout masters before you start making the presentation - If you edit the master after you create individual slides, you'll need to re-apply the changed layouts to the existing slides in your presentation in Normal view. 

Save your own template. You can save your presentation with the customized slide master as your own PowerPoint presentation template (.potx) format. You can then re-use this template and also share it with others to use. So let's see the screen recording of how you can save the edited template as your own template and then how you can use that. 

Follow these steps to save & use your own template: 
So to save it go to the file option, save as, browse and decide where you want to save it and then in the type options select save as PowerPoint template and click save, and that's the way you can save it as your own template. So now when you want to use it, say you're creating a new PowerPoint presentation, you go to new and then there'll be an option for your personal templates and here you can see that the template that you have saved is now available as a template and you can use it to create a whole new presentation. So anyone you share this template with they can use the same process to open and use the new template. 

Diagrams. - You can use diagrams to visually present complex information, thoughts or processes. - PowerPoint has in-built templates for many different types of diagrams. - Some are available through Templates (like we saw earlier) and others are available through SmartArt. 

SmartArt. - Through the SmartArt options in PowerPoint, you can show: Lists, Processes, Cycles, Hierarchies, Relationships, Matrix, Pyramids, Pictures and other options through Office.com. Now let's look at a screen recording on how we can start using SmartArt for infographics and diagrams in PowerPoint. 

Follow these steps to add SmartArt in PowerPoint: 
So if you go into PowerPoint, you can go into the insert tab on the top and click SmartArt and here you can see the different options that they have available for lists, processes, cycles, hierarchy, relationships, matrices, pyramids and then through office.com, and as you click on it all the different options will appear. This is the Public Sector Data Science course where we teach data-related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

In this module, we'll be discussing selecting indicators for rankings. We'll go over the following: First, what is an indicator? Then, choosing indicators followed by questions regarding data collection when you're looking at indicators. We'll then move on to discussing proxy indicators and end with discussing how to develop a criteria for indicator selection. 

At the outset, it's important to note that this module is not exhaustive. There are many different ways to select indicators, and we're just going to be talking through the basics. 

What is an indicator? 
An indicator is a qualitative or quantitative measure that aggregates observed facts and offers a relative position within a defined area. 
In the context of government rankings, we can see two types of indicators: single and composite. 
Single indicators are related to a single aspect of the scheme or programme you are monitoring. For example, number of job cards issued for MGNREGA. 
Composite indicators use a combination of indicators to measure complex issues related to a scheme and its implementation or a sector. For example, the Ease of Doing Business is a composite indicator. 

Choosing indicators 
Creating rankings without adequate context will create data of limited value. Hence, it is important to carefully choose the indicator(s) upon which the ranking is based. 

So as we're choosing an indicator, here are some questions that can help us choose better indicators. First of all, what you will be able to choose would be limited by what is available. Next, like we discussed earlier, what do we want the ranking to mean? And I'll add here, will the ranking hold the same meaning to someone sitting here at the Government of India level as it will for someone at the state, district, or block level? Linked to that, what action do we expect people to take based on the ranking? 
What actions people can take are linked to the next three questions. How frequently the data is updated, how frequently the ranking is updated, and in how much detail we have data available. These three things will help us to decide the periodicity of the ranking and whether it will be something that can prompt short or longer-term action. 

Questions regarding data collection 
We should also consider some questions regarding how the data is collected. We should consider who, when, how, or why. Who is responsible for gathering the data, and who is included and not included in the data? Next, when: which period does the data represent? Will the data be updated in the future and how frequently will it be updated? 
How: how was the data collected? What was the methodology used? Was it a survey? Was there any weighting involved, imputation, modeling, what specific questions were asked? We really need to get into how this data was collected in order to be able to evaluate the indicators in the best possible manner. And lastly, why, for what purpose or purposes was the data collected, and what historic context should be considered? 

Selecting scheme-related indicators 
Because we're talking about creating rankings for government programs, we have to consider the schemes, projects, sectors, or programs within the government context that we're catering to. The process of selection of indicators must take into account the scheme structure, the guidelines, and the policy objectives and priorities. 
Think about which indicators represent scheme inputs and outputs. Take the example of NREGA. Input indicators for this scheme could be budget allocated, funds available, job cards issued, etc. And similarly, output indicators could be total employment provided, women/SC/ST category people employed, works completed, etc. And following from this, you can also try to include outcome indicators that can be measured in a longer term. 

Proxy indicators 
Working in the government, I'm sure you have been in a situation where you wish to measure or evaluate something that is not easily or directly measurable. Proxy indicators are a useful means to address this. For example, you can think of the different things that we measure in government surveys. Like, like for socio-economic well-being, we can look at household assets, or how in Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana, they consider the number of person days a household has worked in NREGA as one of the criteria for access to funds under this scheme. When you're selecting proxy indicators, you should keep in mind that these must be correlated with the indicator, and the higher the correlation, the better the proxy, and second, that the proxy indicator should be able to change in tandem with what you want to evaluate. 

Developing a criteria for indicators 
Based on the scheme you are working on and the data that you collect and access, your team should discuss and decide on a criteria for selecting indicators. Discussing and deciding on this can make your indicator selection more robust. Do document your criteria for selecting indicators so you and your team can refer to it as a guiding principle in the future. 
Some examples of criteria for indicator selection are shared in the next slides. I'm going to be showing those to you, but we'll not be discussing them in detail. You can always refer back to them later, or search for other such indicator criteria on the internet. 

So this one is from New Zealand's Ministry of Social Development. They developed a criteria for selecting indicators that helped them to derive a balanced and manageable set of indicators from the mass of statistics that they had available. So they selected criteria such as how relevant they are to social outcomes, how much support they have, how grounded in research they are, are they able to be disaggregated, are they consistent over times, statistically sound, timely, nationally significant, and internationally comparable. So these are the broad criteria that they selected. Now let's look at another example. 

This example is from USAID's Data for Impact project. Because there are people of various levels of work experience that come into work for them, they decided to create a criteria for indicator selection that people across the organization could access. Creating something like this could be helpful for you as well for different members that are working in your team and also regarding turnover when people come and go so that they all have a common vision that they can think about when choosing indicators for your particular project or scheme or sector. So in the USAID case here, they've selected the following broad themes to consider when selecting indicators: relevance, accuracy, importance, usefulness, feasibility, credibility, validity, and distinctiveness. As you can see, both organizations have some overlaps in the kind of criteria they have set down as guidelines for indicator selection but there are also unique facets that they've added. For example, in New Zealand, they talked about national significance but also international comparability. 

Evaluating indicators in the manner that we just discussed can have relevance way beyond the rankings that we learn how to create. These discussions can contribute to improving your scheme's MIS, dashboards, creating new monitoring mechanisms, improving measurements, and so on. So here we come to the end of this module, and we'll pick up these themes as we discuss ranking of indicators and development of composite indices.

This is the Public Sector Data Science Course, where we teach data-related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

In this module on weighting and aggregating indicators, we'll go over how to weight indicators, creating sub-indices and aggregating the indicators, and lastly, end with things to keep in mind. 

As with the other modules, we will proceed with the same imaginary assignment to create a state performance tracking index for MGNREGA so that officers don't need to refer to different rankings across different indicators and can use a composite index to understand overall performance. 

Building on the previous modules, you have to weight and aggregate the normalized indicators to create a composite index. 

As we had gone over in the previous modules, there are several steps that go into creating a composite index. Now we'll start from the fourth step, which is assigning weightages and proceed on to aggregation to create the index. 

There are a variety of methods that can be used for weighting, ranging from factor analysis to envelopment analysis to participatory weighting techniques. Again, since this course is only providing an introduction, we will not go into all of these methods and you can learn about them through the shared resources at the end of the module. 

Indicators in a CI should be weighted and combined in a manner that reflects the objective and basis for the CI, realities of the scheme, & policy priorities. You can choose to reward (or punish) indicators depending on their significance. If all indicators in a CI are assigned equal weights, it implies that all the indicators are "worth" the same in the CI. This is not recommended because it does not account for the dynamics of scheme implementation and relations between indicators. 

Given the challenges in assigning weights to indicators that will form a CI, weighting decisions can be made by bringing together a group of stakeholders to seek input from different levels of government and also keeping in mind the policy priorities. 

Based on their expertise, experience, and judgement, the group of stakeholders you bring together can decide how to allocate weights adding up to 100. 

The stakeholders should think about things like: which indicators are the most aligned with policy & scheme priorities; how states will react if the weight of certain indicators is increased/decreased; and does assigning a higher weight for one indicator allows states to compensate for poor performance on another? And how does this relate to scheme guidelines and policy priorities? These are just some of the questions that you can use to invigorate the discussion amongst the stakeholders so that they can make an informed decision about how to go about weighting the different indicators for this index. 

Based on the thought process of creating the CI, you can group indicators into sub-indices and take that into consideration when assigning weights. 

The decision to group indicators can be based on: 
1. Underlying basis for the CI (the scheme guidelines and implementation)
2. Factors that may be influencing a particular group of indicators. 

In the case of MGNREGA, indicators relating to provision of employment can be grouped into a sub-index as they are all influenced by the same underlying factors. 

Similarly, in the case of any other scheme, indicators that are all related to one component of the scheme can be grouped. For example, in the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana - Gramin, indicators relating to payments, tranches and timing of payments can all be grouped together. And I'm sure you can think of other such examples from the other schemes that you work with. 

It is advisable to not have too many indicators and sub-indices combined into a single CI. Too many indicators can dilute the role of the indicators being combined and can limit the action that states can take on the basis of the CI. 

For the CI we are developing, based on (hypothetical) stakeholder input, we grouped the indicators into 4 sub-indices. 

Weights (totalling to 100) were assigned to each of the sub-indices as well as the indicators to be combined to create a sub-index. 

So here in this table, you can see how the sub-indices have been created and the weights they've been assigned. 

So the first one is Employment provision, which is made up of two indicators: the percentage of jobcards issued out of applied, and the person days of employment provided per household employed. These are both assigned equal weight 50-50 within the sub-index of Employment provision, which has a weight of 35 in the overall CI. 

The next is Asset creation, which has just one indicator, which is work completion rate, and has a weight of 20. 

The next is Wage payments, which also has only one indicator, which is percentage of transactions completed in stage 1 within 15 days, which has a weight of 35. 

And lastly, Equity, which has two indicators: percentage of Gram Panchayats that have completed at least one social audit in the financial year, and the percentage of SC/ST active workers out of total active workers, which have been weighted 40-60 and together, the Equity sub-index forms 10% of the entire weight. 

Some things to keep in mind while you're going about doing the weighting: 
The stability of the ranking methodology - how sensitive are ranks to changes in the weights assigned to different indicators and sub-components? You should think about how sensitive your ranks are to changes in the weights assigned to different indicators and sub-components. You can check this by updating and playing with the input data and weights assigned and comparing the change in ranks. This itself is an iterative process and you might have to make changes even after you have aggregated all your data. 

Reweighting may need to be done as a result of a change in the scheme guidelines in policy priorities or learning after responses to one iteration of the composite index. 

While this positive learning and adaptation of the index is good, frequent changes in weighting and methodology of the index can reduce its overall stability, as well as its meaning and its ability to prompt action. 

As with normalization and weighting, there is also no standard approach for the selection of an aggregation method. The method you choose should be on the basis of whichever is most suitable for the particular CI that you are building. 

Regardless of which method you choose, you should document your choice, the reasons for doing so and any challenges and assumptions employed in the method. 

This documentation will also be helpful in case you or someone else needs to reconstruct the CI or recalculate the scores to update the index at a later time. 

There are different arithmetic aggregation methods that can be used to combine the indicators, such as additive aggregation method and benchmarking. 

In the additive aggregation method, the calculation of the ranking for each country according to each individual indicator and the summation of the resulting rankings. But by using this, the absolute value of the information is lost. 

The other method of benchmarking is based on the number of indicators that are above and below a given benchmark. This method uses nominal scores for each indicator to calculate the difference between the number of indicators above and below the defined threshold. 

For the purpose of our CI, we will be focusing on the method of summation of normalized and weighted individual indicators. 

In this method, the normalized indicators are summed up according to their given weights. The resulting numbers can then be compared and ranked. If you'd like to know about the process of normalization, please refer to the previous module. 

This is the formula that we will use in Excel to go about summing our weighted normalized scores. 

So we'll start with the numerator, which will have each of the normalized values of the indicators multiplied by their weight and added up, and divided by the sum of the weights. 

Since our CI has 4 sub-indices, we will complete the calculations needed for each of the sub-indices first. 

Since Employment provision and Equity have two indicators within them each, so we will first aggregate these and once we have them aggregated, we will aggregate all of the four sub-indices to create the final CI. 

So like we discussed earlier, we can calculate as per the formula discussed for the two sub-indices which have two indicators each, and it will go something like this: the value for indicator 1 multiplied by the weight assigned for indicator 1 plus the value for indicator 2 multiplied by the weight for indicator 2, add that all up and divided by the sum of the weights, which will be 100. 

And since the weights will be the same for each state, you can fix those values using the dollar signs so that they will remain constant when you drag and apply the formula throughout the column. 

Now let's look at a screen recording to see how you would go about doing this. 

So we'll start with equal to, we'll open the brackets for the numerator. 

We'll select the value for the first indicator multiplied by the weight for the first indicator, close the bracket plus the value for the second indicator multiplied by the weight for the second indicator, close the bracket for the numerator and divide it by the sum of the two weights. 

So now because we want to apply this formula throughout, we'll use the dollar sign to fix the column and cell references so that they will remain constant when you drag and apply the formula throughout the column. 

So now when we apply it throughout, you can see that it's been filled in for all the states. 

So now you can see that we've calculated the sub-indices separately for all of the different indicators. And if you're doing these calculations in different sheets or different workbooks, you can combine them like this into a single table by using the VLOOKUP function that we had discussed in one of the earlier modules on the basic Excel functions. 

Now the same weighted score formula can also be used to combine the sub-indices as per the assigned weights and come up with the total CI value for NREGA and which will fulfill our overall goal for creating an index and a ranking. 

Now let's look at the screen recording to see the steps you will have to follow. 

So we'll start by opening up the brackets for the numerator, the value of the first indicator multiplied by the weight of the first indicator plus the value of the second indicator multiplied by the weight of the second indicator, plus the value of the third indicator multiplied by the weight of the third indicator, and then the value of the fourth indicator multiplied by the weight of the fourth indicator, close the bracket of the numerator and then you divide it, and the denominator will be 100 which is the sum of the weights. 

So as before, we will fix some of the values using the dollar signs because these will remain the same throughout and you can drag and apply the formula to the entire column. 

Now instead of following this long process of selecting each of the indicator values and its, you know, respective weight, you can substitute this by using a built-in Excel function called SUMPRODUCT. 

And as you can see, here is the, you know, the entire formula that we had just used. And if you just use SUMPRODUCT, it will be SUMPRODUCT and it will be indicators multiplied by weights, and in our case we will divide it by 100 because that will be the sum of the weights. 

And this will perform the same function as multiplying the indicators with the weights and then summing them. So this is a formula that brings together this entire process and it's called SUMPRODUCT because it does exactly that, it sums up the product of the value into the weight. 

Now let's look at a screen recording of how this works. 

So we'll write some equal to SUMPRODUCT, open the bracket, select all of the indicator values, comma, all of the weight values, close the bracket and we want to divide it by 100. 

So it's as simple as that. And because we want to apply the formula throughout, we'll fix certain values using the dollar signs because these will remain the same throughout and you can drag and apply the formula to the entire column. 

So now you have the final NREGA CI score for the states, the processes that we have been following in the past few modules have all culminated into the creation of this CI score. 

Now you can present this final CI score for comparisons of states either as a score out of 100, and if you want to do that, you can just not divide the SUMPRODUCT by a 100 or you can multiply it by the sum product of a hundred, you know, some product divided by 100 into 100, which will just cancel out, meaning you just use the SUMPRODUCT, or you can then create a ranking, or you can present both together as I have done here, which will allow the audience to go through the data and also draw their own conclusions of how the rankings have been done, and how the different states have fared in this overall index out of 100. 

So in this case, the ranking should be done in descending order, the higher score should be ranked 1, because a higher CI score indicates a better performance under the selected indicators. But depending on your CI and the data you're using and the meanings and the policy priorities, you will have to decide whether you want to use an ascending or a descending ranking. That totally depends on the type of CI you're creating, the type of indicators you have chosen and the overall objective and meaning of the CI. 

By aggregating the indicators as per their weightage and presenting the final score, there are both gains and losses. One advantage is that now you have a single metric that brings together the different indicators you had chosen and shows how states rank in comparison. 

But, on the other hand, good performance in one indicator can compensate for low performance in another. You can understand this better by seeing the score obtained in the sub-indices. 

So this is a visualization of the table with all of the sub-index data and we've used conditional formatting to apply these colors, and here you can see Tripura, which ranks 2 overall, has one of the lower performances in asset creation. 

But on the other hand, Maharashtra performs very well in wage payments, but is unable to compensate for low performance in all of the other indicators. So you can see how there is a give and take or push and pull across all of the different indicators which come together to form this CI as well as the resulting ranks. 

Through the visualization like this conditional formatting which we had also learned earlier in the data visualization module, you can see that good performance for some indicators compensates for poor performance in others. 

These scores are of course very dependent on the weights assigned to the indicators. You can play around with the weights and see how it affects the scores across the different sub-indices as well as the overall ranking of the states. 

This is the next exercise that your stakeholder group can engage in as they debate and discuss how how weightages should be assigned and how the aggregation method should be followed. 

As the creator of the index, before you publicly release the index or use it for monitoring, you can use such visualizations to see where you can make changes to the CI to make it more beneficial and actionable. 

For example, almost all states are completing stage 1 payments within 15 days, so perhaps this indicator is not the best measure of wage payments and something else needs to be added that is a better indicator. So in this case, perhaps stage 2 payments where they may be more delays or there may be more challenges that require improvement. 

So as we come towards the end of this module, let's think about some things to keep in mind as you are going about the process of weighting and aggregation. 

There is no one way to assign weights to indicators, and we have only covered one example. Since there can be differences of opinion about weighting indicators and aggregating indicators, there is an added layer of subjectivity even with the method of using a participatory approach using various stakeholders. 

To avoid data manipulation and misrepresentation, it's important to keep these methodological issues in mind while creating the composite index, and we'll discuss in the next slide about the need to maintain transparency. 

By keeping these things in mind, you can develop a sound composite index which provides policy-makers with the 'big picture' that they need to make decisions. 

As I'd said earlier, there are many things that you should maintain transparency about to maintain the validity and robustness of your CI. 

You should document and make transparent the details of the weighting methodology and the weights assigned, the details of the sub-indices how and why they were created, and the aggregation techniques used. 

As always, we bring to an end this module by sharing a resource that you can use when you're trying these skills yourself.

So as we come towards the end of this module, let's think about some things to keep in mind as you are going about the process of weighting and aggregation. There is no one way to assign weights to indicators, and we have only covered one example.

There is no one way to assign weights to indicators, and we have only covered one example. Since there can be differences of opinion about weighting indicators and aggregating indicators, there is an added layer of subjectivity even with the method of using a participatory approach using various stakeholders. To avoid data manipulation and misrepresentation, it's important to keep these methodological issues in mind while creating the composite index, and we'll discuss in the next slide about the need to maintain transparency. By keeping these things in mind, you can develop a sound composite index which provides policy-makers with the 'big picture' that they need to make decisions. As I'd said earlier, there are many things that you should maintain transparency about to maintain the validity and robustness of your CI. You should document and make transparent the details of the weighting methodology and the weights assigned, the details of the sub-indices how and why they were created, and the aggregation techniques used. As always, we bring to an end this module by sharing a resource that you can use when you're trying these skills yourself.

1013.lesson_title: Evaluating updating and building confidence in your composite index
1013.text:
This is the Public Sector Data Science Course, where we teach data-related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

In this module, we will learn about evaluating, updating, and building confidence in your composite index. 

This module builds upon the previous few modules that we went through on creating a composite index, where we went through all of these steps, such as determining the need and basis for a composite indicator, evaluation and selection of indicators, normalization, assigning weights, aggregation, and then finally, the display and interpretation of the composite indicator. 

Once the indicator has been created, you may either need to create revisions as a result of feedback from stakeholders or policymakers or states or any other entities that are affected by the index, or there may be changes in scheme guidelines or policy priorities which may again substantiate the need for a change in the index, or the process of updation could be as per the regular cycle where you have decided to update the index at regular intervals and you want to go about doing so. So, there are many reasons why you may feel a need to revisit the index or try to improve it in some manner. 

So, one thing to keep in mind while you are going through all of these things, is to keep in mind, and keep at the forefront, the objective of the CI. Now, the objective of the CI, as we had discussed earlier, must take into account the scheme structure, guidelines, and policy objectives and priorities. And to do this, it's best to look back at the published documents related to the scheme, to look at the latest reports presented on the MIS, to refer back to minutes of meetings from performance reviews, et cetera. And keep this in mind as you go through different stages of creating the CI, as well as while using and updating it. 

Now, to determine how frequently the index has to be updated, think about: the data sources that are being used and how frequently they are updated, think about what actions are expected from the audience of your CI, how frequently can the results of these actions be tracked? If it is meant to review and track state performance, states should be able to act on the results, and whatever metrics they are gaining from the CI. For example, the sanctioning of PMGSY roads is a slow-moving indicator and happens in batches, whereas construction is updated daily. So information like this can help you decide how and when you should be updating the indicators that make up your CI. 

In case you feel the need to add or change any indicators, you can keep the following questions in mind, and we had gone over these questions in the module on selecting indicators. Things like who is responsible for gathering the data, and who is included or not included, which period does the data represent, when will it be updated in the future, how frequently will it be updated, how was the data collected, the methodologies related to it, and for what purposes were the data collected. So again, these are the questions that you should keep in mind, not just while selecting the indicators to create the index in the first place, but also if you are adding anything new, or if you are making any changes as you go forward. 

In the module on weighting and aggregating indicators, we had talked about using a participatory approach and involving stakeholders in discussing and debating and deciding how to assign weights and aggregate the indicators. In fact, you can use a participatory approach throughout, not just in the process of weighting and aggregating, but throughout selecting indicators, selecting the process of normalization, deciding how the indicator is going to be visualized and displayed and shared by states or the entities being ranked, or even with the general public. And like we had discussed earlier, these stakeholders should have both experience and expertise in areas related to the indicators chosen and the scheme chosen, and represent different levels of government. 

Now, when you go about actually updating the composite index, you should think about, like I had said earlier, the objective of the index, the indicators chosen, as well as the periodicity of the data used. Now, one thing to keep in mind is that it would be best if the weights remain constant, even while you update. Otherwise, it will be unclear whether any change in rankings is due to change in performance, or due to the change in the weights assigned. And this can be quite confusing as well as misleading. If the weights do need to change, for example, due to change in policy priorities, this should be highlighted and documented and made transparent. Changing the methodology used, and the weighting and aggregating methods used in a CI can be quite demotivating to the entities being ranked, and eventually, lessen the impact of the CI overall. 

From a pragmatic point of view, it may not be possible to create a composite index that is perfect in all regards, and compromises will often need to be made. So, as we have said in previous modules as well, transparency is key. 

You can be transparent by providing information about the reason for choosing indicators and their data sources, details about missing values, data dropped, and imputations, the methods used for normalization and why you chose a particular method, details of the weighting methodology and the weights assigned, and if you are going using a participatory approach, who were the stakeholders involved in this process, the details of the sub-indices that have been created and why particular indicators were grouped together and what was the reasoning behind that, what is the aggregation technique that you have used and why, and then lastly, the updation frequency and any changes that are made in the methodology as you go forward. 

Now, once your composite index is made, as well as during the process of creating the composite index, there are several steps that you can take to build confidence in your index so that people are comfortable using it and it carries weight. The first is to publish granular data of the indicators used to create the CI, so that users can see right away what they can work on to improve the ranking. Next, you can present detailed information about the weighting of indicators and sub-indices, and when you update the index, also share information about why and how weights were changed in case they had to be changed. You should account for the differences in those being ranked and the effects on performance. For example, large vs small states will vary in their performance, and you should take such things into account. You should perform statistical checks on the data to see correlations between indicators, effects of weighting on rankings, and changes in ranking after change in methodology. 

To sum up, if designed well, rankings can draw attention to gaps in policy implementation, assist in decision-making and resource allocation, initiate learning effects among those being ranked, foster competition between those being ranked. And in case they are not designed well, rankings can lead to an oversimplification of complex government challenges and demotivate those who rank poorly. 

This brings us to the end of this module. As always, here are some resources and references that you can look at when you work on implementing these skills.
