659.text:
Welcome to this session of principles of data collection. As you all might have gone through various parts of this course, wherein, we have been teaching you about how you develop your research proposal, how you write your protocol, and now you have gone through all that and you are all set to collect your data. Let me tell you that this is one of the most most important component of your research study because this is what is going to determine what you get out of your data.

So today, as we go through this lecture, let me discuss about two main principles of data quality, which is reliability and accuracy. So, reliability, what does it really mean? It means that your study should have repeatability and precision. What it means? If this same study is repeated by different investigators or the same measurement is done by different at different time points, you should still be able to get more or less similar results. It also refers to stability and consistency of the information. Now, reliability does not ensure that your data is accurate. Accuracy accuracy refers to ability of a measurement to be correct.

It could happen that the both the attributes may not happen at the same time or they may happen. So, let me give you an example of what would be the various scenario in terms of data quality. As you can see in this slide, your study might give you reliable and accurate result, which means your data is giving the measurement that you really want. Their measurement is accurate and repeatable. Now, this is an ideal case scenario. The worst case scenario is that your measurement may not be reliable at all and may not be accurate also. Now, there can be other scenarios, where your measurement is reliable, that is if you repeat this measurement again and again, you get the same measurement, same kind of result repeatedly. However, this could still not be accurate. And there can be another scenario that you may get the accurate result, but when somebody tries to repeat this experiment, you may not be able to repeat it at all. So, an ideal study should ensure that whatever outcome you are measuring is repeatable as well as it is accurate. Now to ensure that, we can follow certain principles of data collection.

So, in today's lecture, we will be going through six broad principles which are listed here. I will be walking you through each of these principles. So, the first is, as you have your questionnaire ready, and you are all set to start your data collection, one more step you need to do is, you need to develop a guide. Guide wherein for each of the questions, you can have a small explanation as to how this data actually need to be collected. The second component that we will talk about is how you could do a good training of your staff members to ensure that the data quality is good. The third component is how do you ensure data quality when the work has already been initiated, it could be in a clinic setting or it could be in the field. And the next component is how you need to do periodic reviews to ensure good quality of your data. In during this process, it may happen that your staff will come across various difficulties in data collection, and you need to have periodic debriefing for that, and finally and very very important component is how you validate that your study results are actually correct. So let's go over each of these components one by one.

So what do you really mean by a question-by-question guide? It's nothing but a short, simple document, which is a guide for your field worker or your clinic research staff, or whoever is involved in the data collection. Now why is this an important component? Everybody may not understand the question in the same way. A different individuals or your staff members may have their own interpretations as to how this question need to be asked and how it need to be explained to the respondent. The Q-by-Q guide ensures that all the investigators uniformly ask the question and they all understand the question in the same way. What do you do here? You just take your questionnaire and write a short explanation under each of your question as to how this question should be asked and what could be the possible responses and in certain situations you may have some probes. You would like the investigator to probe little more on a particular question. If you want them to do so you you would like to make a mention of that. Similarly, it allows you to explain where they should skip, where they should give more emphasis. All this guidance can be given through this small document.

This not only provides a guide as to how data should be collected, but it is a road map. And at any point of time, whenever there is a doubt, whenever there is a lack of consistency within an investigator, you can always ask them to go back to this document to ensure that the data collection is being done in a uniform way. Now, it could happen that as you start collecting data, you may come across certain difficulties in the field, and you may have to revise this guide which is all right, and what is important is whatever changes are done, they should be documented in this Q-by-Q guide at that point of time.

This is just to show you an example. For example, you have a question on what is the type of house, right? We could give several options. Okay, this is a kaccha house, it's a semi-pakka house, or a pakka house. Everybody may not understand what is a kaccha house. So, you may want to give an explanation. Observe the house and note if it is made of mud or bricks. And then you could write an explanation: If you find that the house is made of mud, then mark it as a kaccha house. Similarly, another example, when you are asking a question regarding household income. Now, it could happen that in a particular household, there are more than one members, who are earning members of the family, and in this situation, you would like your investigators to first of all inquire how many earning members are there in the family, then they need to find out each one of them how much they earn, and what is their monthly income. They need to add up all that amount and then write the answer as, what is the total household income. So, similarly for each question, you can have the detailed explanation.

Now coming to, once your Q-by-Q guide is ready, you are all set to start your data collection. Before you get on the ground, whether it's a clinic, whether it's a field based study, it's a household study, whatever will be the type of study, training. Good training is essential to ensure that the quality of data is good. And in that, the first and foremost step is choosing right kind of people. You need to understand what your study requirements are and depending on the study requirements, you need to recruit or select right kind of investigators. Now this could be depending on, suppose you are doing a study which is on clinical research, then you need to make sure that your investigators know how to ask the clinical questions, are they knowing how to use the clinical terms when they are interacting with the patient? If it is a field based study, you need to make sure that your investigators are familiar with the local language. They know how to culturally interact with the people at the community level. So, selecting the right kind of investigator, who will be suitable for your data collection, is the most important step. Once you have done that, you need to have a classroom session with them. This is nothing but walking them through your first of all, you introduce them to what your study is all about. Why are you doing this study? What are your objectives? And what is that you would like them to know, the basics of what what are the various definition you are using in the study, what are the various component of the study, what is the kind of data that needs to be collected. For example, your study may have different component, there could be a questionnaire, there could be different measurements. Maybe you want them to measure something like weight, height, so you need to familiarize them what are the various kinds of data collection that they need to do. Once you have done that and given them the overview, then you need to share this Q-by-Q guide, question-by-question guide, walk them through each question, allow them to ask questions, and let them go through it and see whether they are able to interpret those questions, whether they are able to understand those questions. Once they have done that, you need to tell them what exactly they need to do in the field, how they need to ask those questions, and what should be the explanation that they should understand before they ask the questions. Now as a first step, having gone through this exercise, you would like them to probably do these interviews, first of all in the classroom, wherein one of the investigators could act as the interviewer and the another investigator could be the respondent, and they should simulate this in front of you, which allows you to guide them, to tell them how the question need to be asked, whether the question is being understood by the respondent, whether the question is being asked in the appropriate language that is given in the questionnaire.

Having done that, you are all set now to do your final data collection. Here, what is very important is that you need to plan your team structure. So there has to be a supervisor who could be present all the time or who could be present periodically, along with the investigators. Ensure that the study forms are verified by the supervisor every day. Now why is this important? Because once you have left the clinic, or once you have left the village or the place where you are doing the data collection, some of the errors cannot be corrected. During, as the data collection starts, they may come up with different queries. So, you need to be available to answer those questions. This could be over the phone, this could be over the messages, or whatever way you can use. Now once the data collection is ongoing, the next step that as a principle investigator, you need to do is, few on-site visits to ensure that the data collection is done as per the protocol and the questionnaire is being actually used in the field the way you had perceived it.

I think one of the important thing you need to keep in mind is, very often what happens is there are time pressures, you want to finish your study quickly, you want to be done with it. You may pressurize them, you may say, oh, I would like you to do 10 questionnaire every day. However, you need to make sure that the quality is not diluted because you are pressing them to work under very tight timelines.

Having done this, having your data collection, so as the data collection goes on, at various time points, you may want to review, suppose let's say you have already collected now 50 forms. At this stage, you may want to make sure that the data collected is of good quality and the data is complete. How can you do that? The first step can be done in the field itself. As your supervisor finishes finishes the day, he can collect all the forms from various team members and check them on that day itself. The next step is the forms will reach you as a principle investigator, and you need to go through them to make sure that you are satisfied with the quality of data.

What kind of checks you can conduct when you have got the forms in your hand? I think the first and foremost and the most easiest one, but the most important one is, ensure there are no blanks. It could happen that when they are asking multiple question, since your questionnaire may have about 20 question or 25 questions, they may just forgot to ask a few questions, or they may have asked the question but they did not mark it in the questionnaire, but in either case you will see them as a blank. So you need to ensure completeness of the data. The second is, readability. Sometimes the way it is marked, it may be hard for you to even understand and some of the answers could have some actual explanation to be written. Some, some kind of clinical symptoms or some kind of narratives have to be written, ensure that those things are readable. The next is the consistency, does the answer make sense? Do you feel that this could be the way the people would have answered, or you got this answer because maybe your respondents were not understanding the questions.

Periodic reviews are essential in case of any study, whether it's a clinical study, it's a field study or any type of research study. Now these regular meetings, one it could be done by the supervisor, which could be in the field itself or after coming back or you can have a periodic review, once in a week, once in a month, depending on what is the duration of your study. What is that these review meetings will be useful for? First of all, to clarify, if there are any queries they have about the questionnaires, if they understand the questions well, if they came across something which they had not anticipated. Now it may happen that during these meetings you may end up doing some changes in the way your answers are drafted or in the way questions are asked. If you are doing that, ensure that these are well documented and they are added it in your Q-by-Q guide.

Now coming to the last, but not the least, very very important component of data collection which is validation of your data. How can this be done? So for any study, a small sub-sample, it could be as small as even 5% should be selected and an independent second interview should be done. This is to ensure that the data collected by your investigator is actually valid. By comparing the results you will be able to find out if there are any discrepancies, if somebody has made any major errors or it could be that a particular investigator might have been repeating certain errors, or it may happen certain errors are repetitive across the team. So, depending on whatever the problem is, you may want to discuss this with the individual team member or with all the study team.

So just to sum up, what we have gone through today, before you get on to your data collection, understand the concepts of data quality, good training, both in the classroom as well as on-site in a similar setting where you are going to conduct the study, is essential for a good research study and supportive supervision, team work are key to good quality data collection. Thank you very much.

Before you get on the ground, whether it's a clinic, whether it's a field based study, it's a household study, whatever will be the type of study, training. Good training is essential to ensure that the quality of data is good. And in that, the first and foremost step is choosing right kind of people. You need to understand what your study requirements are and depending on the study requirements, you need to recruit or select right kind of investigators. Now this could be depending on, suppose you are doing a study which is on clinical research, then you need to make sure that your investigators know how to ask the clinical questions, are they knowing how to use the clinical terms when they are interacting with the patient? If it is a field based study, you need to make sure that your investigators are familiar with the local language. They know how to culturally interact with the people at the community level. So, selecting the right kind of investigator, who will be suitable for your data collection, is the most important step.

So, selecting the right kind of investigator, who will be suitable for your data collection, is the most important step. Once you have done that, you need to have a classroom session with them. This is nothing but walking them through your first of all, you introduce them to what your study is all about. Why are you doing this study? What are your objectives? And what is that you would like them to know, the basics of what what are the various definition you are using in the study, what are the various component of the study, what is the kind of data that needs to be collected. For example, your study may have different component, there could be a questionnaire, there could be different measurements. Maybe you want them to measure something like weight, height, so you need to familiarize them what are the various kinds of data collection that they need to do. Once you have done that and given them the overview, then you need to share this Q-by-Q guide, question-by-question guide, walk them through each question, allow them to ask questions, and let them go through it and see whether they are able to interpret those questions, whether they are able to understand those questions.

Once they have done that, you need to tell them what exactly they need to do in the field, how they need to ask those questions, and what should be the explanation that they should understand before they ask the questions. Now as a first step, having gone through this exercise, you would like them to probably do these interviews, first of all in the classroom, wherein one of the investigators could act as the interviewer and the another investigator could be the respondent, and they should simulate this in front of you, which allows you to guide them, to tell them how the question need to be asked, whether the question is being understood by the respondent, whether the question is being asked in the appropriate language that is given in the questionnaire. Having done that, you are all set now to do your final data collection. Here, what is very important is that you need to plan your team structure. So there has to be a supervisor who could be present all the time or who could be present periodically, along with the investigators. Ensure that the study forms are verified by the supervisor every day. Now why is this important?

Ensure that the study forms are verified by the supervisor every day. Now why is this important? Because once you have left the clinic, or once you have left the village or the place where you are doing the data collection, some of the errors cannot be corrected. During, as the data collection starts, they may come up with different queries. So, you need to be available to answer those questions. This could be over the phone, this could be over the messages, or whatever way you can use. Now once the data collection is ongoing, the next step that as a principle investigator, you need to do is, few on-site visits to ensure that the data collection is done as per the protocol and the questionnaire is being actually used in the field the way you had perceived it. I think one of the important thing you need to keep in mind is, very often what happens is there are time pressures, you want to finish your study quickly, you want to be done with it. You may pressurize them, you may say, oh, I would like you to do 10 questionnaire every day. However, you need to make sure that the quality is not diluted because you are pressing them to work under very tight timelines.

However, you need to make sure that the quality is not diluted because you are pressing them to work under very tight timelines. At this stage, you may want to make sure that the data collected is of good quality and the data is complete. How can you do that? The first step can be done in the field itself. As your supervisor finishes finishes the day, he can collect all the forms from various team members and check them on that day itself. The next step is the forms will reach you as a principle investigator, and you need to go through them to make sure that you are satisfied with the quality of data. What kind of checks you can conduct when you have got the forms in your hand? I think the first and foremost and the most easiest one, but the most important one is, ensure there are no blanks.

I think the first and foremost and the most easiest one, but the most important one is, ensure there are no blanks. It could happen that when they are asking multiple question, since your questionnaire may have about 20 question or 25 questions, they may just forgot to ask a few questions, or they may have asked the question but they did not mark it in the questionnaire, but in either case you will see them as a blank. So you need to ensure completeness of the data. The second is, readability. Sometimes the way it is marked, it may be hard for you to even understand and some of the answers could have some actual explanation to be written. Some, some kind of clinical symptoms or some kind of narratives have to be written, ensure that those things are readable. The next is the consistency, does the answer make sense? Do you feel that this could be the way the people would have answered, or you got this answer because maybe your respondents were not understanding the questions. Periodic reviews are essential in case of any study, whether it's a clinical study, it's a field study or any type of research study.

Periodic reviews are essential in case of any study, whether it's a clinical study, it's a field study or any type of research study. Now these regular meetings, one it could be done by the supervisor, which could be in the field itself or after coming back or you can have a periodic review, once in a week, once in a month, depending on what is the duration of your study. What is that these review meetings will be useful for? First of all, to clarify, if there are any queries they have about the questionnaires, if they understand the questions well, if they came across something which they had not anticipated. Now it may happen that during these meetings you may end up doing some changes in the way your answers are drafted or in the way questions are asked. If you are doing that, ensure that these are well documented and they are added it in your Q-by-Q guide. Now coming to the last, but not the least, very very important component of data collection which is validation of your data. How can this be done? So for any study, a small sub-sample, it could be as small as even 5% should be selected and an independent second interview should be done.

So for any study, a small sub-sample, it could be as small as even 5% should be selected and an independent second interview should be done. This is to ensure that the data collected by your investigator is actually valid. By comparing the results you will be able to find out if there are any discrepancies, if somebody has made any major errors or it could be that a particular investigator might have been repeating certain errors, or it may happen certain errors are repetitive across the team. So, depending on whatever the problem is, you may want to discuss this with the individual team member or with all the study team. So just to sum up, what we have gone through today, before you get on to your data collection, understand the concepts of data quality, good training, both in the classroom as well as on-site in a similar setting where you are going to conduct the study, is essential for a good research study and supportive supervision, team work are key to good quality data collection. Thank you very much.

00:00 This is the Public Sector Data Science course where we teach data related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

00:13 In part II of this module on the Basics of Excel, we'll learn how to use Text to Columns to split data. We learn how to use this Flash Fill feature on Excel and we learn how to combine data using VLOOKUP. 

00:30 As always, we'll start by describing a hypothetical situation which are likely to experience in the government context and then we'll go about learning the skills that we would we would use to address it. 

00:41 So imagine you're working for an office which is involved with the monitoring and management of roads that are constructed under the PMGSY scheme. 

00:50 You have to use the data from the scheme's National Management Information System (MIS) to conduct your analysis. 

00:55 But because of the format that the MIS data is in, you have to first clean the data and then you have to combine it with another data set to get more detailed information. So now we'll see how we'll go about doing this. 

01:07 In the first module of this series, we looked at how to clean the data that we download from the MIS. 

01:14 If you had followed the steps discussed in that module, you would have by now removed the formatting, removed the blank rows and the columns in the data, removed the merge cells and figure out how to fill in the blank values. 

01:28 Now we're ready to start the analysis. But if you look at the column highlighted with the red rectangle, here you can see that the two dates that we need to use for our analysis are combined together into one column. 

01:40 The columns named Voucher period shows the date from which the voucher period starts and the date on which it ends. 

01:47 But for us to use it as part of our analysis, we need to split it into two columns. 

01:53 Now, this example is from PMGSY. But if you look at data from other schemes, you'll find similar examples like this, where multiple data points that you want to use for your analysis are clubbed together into one column. 

02:04 So we'll be using the Text to Columns feature in Excel to split this data into two columns. 

02:12 Using the Text to Column feature, text can be split into multiple columns using delimiters. Delimiters used could be space, comma, tab, full stop, etc. You will have to see what is used in the data that you want to split. 

02:42 How the text gets split will depend on what delimiters you select. And you'll see exactly how to do this when I show you on Excel. 

02:54 Text to columns can also be used when you have to split things like: Name into First Name and Last Name, Split date & time data into separate columns, Remove unit from number (eg: split Rs.100 to Rs and 100). 

03:34 So the data that we looked at in the PMGSY data sheet, we need to split this into three parts based on where the spaces are. 

03:43 So there's the first date, a space, TO space and then the second date. 

03:49 So we'll be using the places where these spaces occur as the delimiters within the Text to Columns feature in order to split the data into different columns. And now I'll show you a screen recording to show you exactly how to do it on Excel. 

04:08 So we'll start with first adding two blank columns where this data will get split. Then we'll select the column we want to split, go to the Data tab, and select Text to Columns. 

04:21 A dialog box will appear, and here we'll select Delimited, and click Next at the bottom. And we'll select Space as our type of delimiter and click Next. 

04:36 At the bottom you'll be able to see the preview of how the data will be split, and if that looks fine you can click Finish to execute the split. So the data will get split like this and we don't need the two column, so we can just delete that. 

04:59 So this is what the data will look like after you finished the text to column splitting and deleting the two column with the data that we don't need. 

05:12 The Flash Fill feature can be used to fill data in a sheet. Excel senses a pattern based on what you enter and executes the rest of the selected rows/columns as per that. 

05:15 It can be used instead of the Text to Columns feature we learned earlier or instead of the =TRIM(_) function as well. 

05:23 You can use it for names, IDs, addresses, dates, etc. 

05:45 So like before, first you insert two columns. And we want to split it into the first date and the second date, so we'll just paste in the first date and then paste in the second date because this is the format we want it to be in. 

06:03 Now we'll select the cell below, go to the Data tab and click Flash Fill. And immediately you can see Excel has followed the pattern and filled in the rest of the data in the same format. 

06:25 When dealing with government data, two types of information that we want to look at or analyse together could be in two different tables in the MIS. 

06:30 So how do we combine these and bring them together for analysis? The most important thing we need is a common, unique variable that we can use to link the two sets of data. 

07:19 We have one data set with detailed information about payments made for roads but we don't have the information about which blocks and Project Implementation Units (PIUs) these roads fall into. 

07:39 So imagine that your reporting officer asked for a block-wise breakdown of the payments made. 

07:44 It'll be such a time consuming task to either cross-reference each row of information and figure out which block it belongs to, or you can go down the other route where you ask each of the blocks to collate their own data and send it to you so that you can combine it. 

07:59 But this can easily be dealt with by compiling the road-wise information with the block and PIU names if we have a common identifier using the VLOOKUP function on Excel. 

08:10 So in the first data set we want to use, we have the road-wise data on how much payment was done and on which date. And here with the red rectangle, I've highlighted the package number, because this is what we'll be using as our unique identifier, because there's a unique package number for each road. 

08:29 And in the second data set we have the block and PIU name for each road, and this is the important information that you that we need. And here you can see that this data set also has the package numbers. So this is the unique identifier that we'll be using to combine these two data sets. 

08:45 We want to combine the data from the two sheets and present it in this format. So now I've created a format with two columns, title block and PIU, and this is where we'll be filling in the information by using the package number as the reference. 

09:05 = VLOOKUP (lookup value, range containing the lookup value, the column number in the range containing the return value, Approximate match (TRUE) or Exact match (FALSE)). Here the lookup value will be the package number of the road and the column containing the return value will first be the column with the block names and then the column with the PIU names. 

10:14 VLOOKUP formula will search for the Package No. and will return the corresponding Block name from the other list. The same process will be followed for the PIU name. 

10:25 The mandatory condition for using VLOOKUP is that the data that will be searched (in this case the Package Number) should be present in the left most column. 

10:41 Hence, we will move the Package Number column to the first column position. 

10:57 The first thing we'll do is move the package number column to the left most column of the sheet. 

11:07 Then we'll go to the sheet that has the format we want to put the data into and start typing in the VLOOKUP function. We'll type in VLOOKUP open the bracket. First will be the lookup value which is the package number. 

11:19 Then the entire table that contains the number where we'll be looking up the values, followed by the column number where the block names are so in this case it's 4, and then false for the exact match. 

11:34 Then you'll follow the same steps for the PIU name. Type in = VLOOKUP, lookup value, and then the table array, which you can use the command shift, right arrow key and then down arrow key, and then 5 for the column with the PIU names and then false for exact match. 

12:07 Now to apply the formula to the entire columns, we'll use the dollar signs to fix the cell references so that they don't change as the formula is applied down through the entire column. 

12:22 So we'll fix the values for the block names, and then click on the corner of the cell to apply it to the entire column. And then similarly use the dollar signs to fix the values for the VLOOKUP function for the PIU name. 

12:43 And then after doing that again, click on the corner of the cell to apply it to the entire column. 

12:53 The final list after using VLOOKUP will appear as below: 

13:03 How to split and extract data from columns, Amazing things Text to Columns can do for you, How to use the VLOOKUP function.

998.text: Public Sector Data Science Course. 2022. Everyday Data Science, using PivotTables to analyse scheme data. PivotTables, what we'll learn: Basics of PivotTables, Grouping data in a PivotTable, Using value functions in a PivotTable, Adding Filters and Slicers, Making PivotCharts. Exercise: You have been asked to analyse Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (DDUGKY) placement data ahead of a meeting. You need to understand trends in employment across sectors. We'll start by describing a hypothetical situation that you are likely to experience in the government context in India, and then we'll go about discussing the skills we would need to address it. Although we are using an example from a particular scheme, the skills that we will discuss can be generalized. In this case, your reporting officer has asked you to analyse the DDUGKY scheme placement data before a meeting, and you have to understand the trends in employment and salaries across sectors. What is a PivotTable? It is an interactive table that allows you to summarise your data. It can be used to segment and compare data. It can be used to look at the same data from different perspectives. It presents the analysis in an easy to understand format. You can build in filters or slicers so that the same table can include different data as needed. Preparing data for a PivotTable: Clean data - Remove formatting, One observation per row. Unique and useful column headers. Data should not already be in summary format. Data for a PivotTable. To understand how candidate salaries vary and potential reasons for variation, we will explore the following questions using PivotTables: Which sectors and trades are majority of the candidates employed in? What is the average salary across each sector/designation? Candidates per sector. Follow these steps to create the PivotTable: Click anywhere within your data set on Excel, then go to the Insert tab and click PivotTable. You will also see a recommended PivotTables option. Click on this to see which tables Excel has automatically created for your data. Select PivotTable. Select the range for your data. Select where you want the table to appear. Click OK. We will use these PivotTable fields options to build our PivotTable. You can use the settings icons to decide how you want the fields to appear. Since we want to create a table which lists the sectors, drag the sector_name option to the ROWS box on the right. By doing this, the list of sector names will appear in rows in the first column. Now we need to add the number of individual candidates who are employed in each sector. Each individual is represented by their unique ID in our data set (unique_candidate), so we can use this variable to "count" the number of individuals employed in each sector. Drag and drop the unique_candidate variable to the VALUES box. Select the PivotTable headers to edit them, so that they better reflect the content of the table. Right click on the data to change the number format and sort the data. Format Cells. In this case we want to use the thousand separator and click OK. You can again right click to change the formatting in case you want to remove the decimal places. And you can also use the same right click option to sort the data. So in this case, we've sorted it from largest to smallest so that the sector with the largest number of candidates appears at the very top. From this we can see that the largest number of candidates are employed in the Apparel sector, followed by IT-TES and Retail. Instead of using the total number of candidates per sector, we can better understand the proportion of total candidates employed in that sector out of the total number of candidates. We can show this information in the PivotTable we just created by calculating the percentages. Follow these steps to show the percentage of total candidates: Right click. Show Values As, and click Percent of Grand Total. This will immediately give you the percentage values for each sector. From this we can see that 41.56% of candidates are employed in the Apparel sector, 9.83% in the IT-ES sector and 8.24% in the Retail sector. And these are the insights that you can quickly draw by creating a pivot table. And I'm sure you can think of other applications from the scheme data that you work with. To further look at the break-up of the type of roles (designations) within these sectors that candidates are employed in, we can add the sector-wise designation break-down to the pivot table. As per what is needed - you can also add the break-down in terms of trade names, designations, etc. This is also called "grouping" the data within a PivotTable. Follow these steps to add the break-down to the Pivot Table: To see the break-down of the designation, drag the designation item into the ROWS box on the right. Immediately you can see the plus and minus boxes under each of the sectors and here I am closing them to show you how they all get collapsed and grouped. When we created the initial PivotTable, we used the COUNT value of the candidate IDs to come up with the count of the candidates in each sector. In a PivotTable, you can also use other value functions such as SUM, AVERAGE etc. To demonstrate, let's see how we can add the average salary for each designation in another column in the Pivot Table. To see the average salary for each designation under each sector, drag the salary variable to the VALUES box. In the VALUES box, you will see Sum of salary. Since we want the salaries to be shown as averages, we can change the manner in which the values for salary are shown by changing the Value Field Settings. To change the Value Field Settings for Sum of salary, click on the drop down arrow, and select Value Field Settings. The Value Field Settings box will open. Select Average under the Summarize value field by option. Then click OK. Follow these steps to add average salaries to the Pivot Table: We'll drag the salary, Sum of salary will appear. Click on the arrow, say Value Field Settings, the pop up will appear. We click Average and select OK. And as soon as we do that you can see that the average salary has appeared and you can change the number format. And you can again right click to change the formatting in case you want to remove the decimal places. And like I'd shown you before you can also right click and sort the values. The output will appear as follow: The average salary column has been formatted by right-clicking and using the Number Format and Sort (descending) options. In another module we had also discussed the challenges of relying on the average value as an indicator of the distribution and central tendency of the data. So along with this we can also show the Minimum and Maximum salaries since these functions are also built into the Value Field Settings for PivotTables. Adding a filter: Since reading the charts with the +/- drop down options for designations under each sector can become cumbersome, we can develop simpler looking PivotTables to see detailed data under each sector individually by using the PivotTable Filter option. By using the filter option we can create individual tables for each sector with just one click. Follow these steps to add filters to the Pivot Table: Click on your table and then all you have to do is drag the sector name if to the filters box. As soon as you do that, the sector names will appear as a filter, and you can use the drop down to select which sector you want to create the pivot chart for. 1003.lesson_title: Data Tables Spark Lines and Conditional Formatting
1003.text:
Welcome to this public sector data science course where we'll teach data-related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

In this module, we'll be continuing to learn about data visualization. We'll cover using tables to communicate data, then learn about sparklines and columns, and end with learning about conditional formatting. 

In this module, we'll be focusing on tables with different types of formatting and merge with data-visualized elements to present your data. 

When are data tables more helpful than visualizations? 
In fact, it is a form of visualization. In review or discussion meetings, a printout of data may be more useful than a presentation with visualizations. You can pack in a lot of information and retain details that you may otherwise lose in a chart. In this module, we'll go through some steps to format tables so that they are easy to read and understand and learn how to use spark lines and conditional formatting to visually highlight the data in the table. 

Let's go over the basics for formatting a table. 
Try to always right-align the data in columns so that the units, tens, hundreds, and thousands are aligned and easily comparable. 
Round the numbers consistently. If decimal points are relevant, then usually don't show more than 2 decimal digits, otherwise it becomes hard for your audience to comprehend them. 
You should remove any unimportant or irrelevant information, but continue to keep the detail in your data. 
The total values for your data and the different columns can be presented at the top or bottom of the table depending on their relevance. 

You should use the same measure across all the data in the table. If both measures, like number of beneficiaries and percentages, are being used in the same table, then make that clear in the column headings. 
Write the units when they're being used in the top right corner if the unit is the same for the whole table, and in the column heading if it's different across columns. For example, if in one column you're using number of roads, and in another column you're using length of roads, the number one should be specified as the number and the length should be specified that it's in kilometers. 
The title of the table should be clear and concise. If the data is for a particular time period or till a particular date, then that should be mentioned in the title. 

Try to create order in your table. Depending on what is relevant, you can use alphabetical order, use ascending or descending order. 
You can merge columns to show grouping of data. For example, if you're showing the number of active beneficiaries by gender, caste, and then total beneficiaries, you can show them in different groups. 
Merge when presenting the data but not when analyzing, because this will affect how clean your data is and how you can apply your summary statistics formulas. 
Keep the font and font sizing of all the values in your table the same. This is unless you're using something different to place emphasis, like making certain values bold or in italics. 

Let's start now with looking at sparklines and columns in tables. 
Sparklines and columns are tiny little charts created in an Excel cell that can show data trends. These can be used to show data trends visually within a table format. Now, let's look at a screen recording to show you how to implement this in Excel. 

To insert sparklines on your table, go to insert, click lines, select the data range for which you want to show the sparklines, then show the location line range of where you want the lines to be inserted, and click okay. And you can see how the lines have been inserted. 

Now, let's see how to insert columns. Click the column option, again, select the data for which you want to create the columns, and again, you can select the range where you want the columns to appear. Here, you can see what the columns look like. 
Now, let me just go back and show you the sparklines again. So, I'll click Insert, lines, again, select the range for which I want the lines, the location for where I want the lines to appear, and now let me show you how you can format these lines. If you click on them, there will be options to format them in the design tab. You can change the color, you can add highlight points, which show you where the highest point in your data is. You can also decide to show the lowest points. 
Changing the color and adding the highest or lowest points can add emphasis to your data and make it even easier for your audience to see how the data is changing. 

You can think of sparklines as mini line or time series charts, and the columns as mini column charts, but without all the other features of a chart that we'd otherwise learn how to use. You can use the format options like I'd shown in the screen recording in the previous slide to make the data more eye-catching, or to draw attention to things like high/low points, etc. 

Now, let's move on to conditional formatting. 
When should you use a table with conditional formatting? 
For data sets where a table will convey information easily, rather than using a chart, conditional formatting can be used. It can be used to group and compare data in a set and show the analytical idea behind the table, and how comparisons can be made. 
Adding conditional formatting to a table will help give a visual idea of where the audience should focus, and make the discussion of the data much easier. It's very useful for when you're creating printouts that have to be used in a meeting or discussion. 

So, let's see how you can start using the conditional formatting option in Excel. So, if you click the conditional formatting option that you see in the data ribbon on the very top, after you select your data in Excel, you will see that there are multiple options that you can use, like highlighting cells based on rules, highlighting just the top or bottom x% of your data, using color scales, like what you saw in the previous slide, and inserting icons. 
Below all of that, there are options for you to create new rules based on the conditional formatting that you want to apply. You can see the options there, like new rule, clear rules, and manage rules. These are the options that you can use to make a new rule, remove that rule, and then also create edits to those rules. 

So, the conditional formatting options also have pre-defined rules within them. So, in the visual shown on the right, you can see the preset rules that are already there. So, for example, if you clicked Highlight Cell Rules, you can already see that there are options that you can use to automatically highlight cells that are greater than a particular number, less than a particular number, between two different numbers, equal to a particular number, or highlight text that contains something, or a particular date that occurs, or even highlight duplicate values. And then there's options to create your own rules to do the same thing. 
So, let me now next show you a screen recording on how to add color scales for the different columns within a table where you want to apply conditional formatting. So, let's go on to see the screen recording. 
So, here we start with selecting the column where we want to apply the conditional formatting, click Conditional Formatting, and here we want to apply color scales. Here, so we'll select that option. And you can see that there are built-in different combinations of the color scales. So, we'll select the one with red, yellow, and green. And that's what it looks like once the built-in rules for the color scale conditional formatting is applied to one column. 
You can repeat this same process to apply the same color scale conditional formatting to all three columns. 

This table is not very helpful for us because the automatic color scales have applied red to the lowest values to show that they are "bad" and green to the highest values to show that they are "good." 
But in our case, it's actually the opposite. The green values which are less, means that it's taken less number of days for an SHG to open their bank account, which means that's good because it's taken less time. 
And red shows the higher number of days, which means it's bad. They're taking too long to open their bank accounts. 
So, we can actually edit the rules in the conditional formatting of the color scales to show and convey the information that we actually want. 
So, let me now show you a screen recording on Excel to show you how you can go about editing the rules and changing the way that the color scales are represented. 

So, here let's select the place where we already applied the color scale, say Manage Rules, and then select Edit Rules, and these options will appear. So, now we want the lowest values to become green, instead of red. We'll leave the midpoint as yellow, and we'll make the maximum values as red. 
So, now the color scale has changed and you can apply it and you can see how the changes have been applied. 
You can repeat the same process to implement the changes in the color scales for the other two columns as well. 

After editing the color scales, it will appear as follows. But remember that you need to sort your data. So, in the first column, you can see I've already sorted the data and you can proceed to do the same for the other two columns, or however you feel like the data can be best sorted. 
When you look at this data table with the conditional formatting, you can immediately see that Deoghar, which is the last in the table, ranks the last in the number of days to open a bank account but takes the fewest days for RF distribution. If you look at the last row, you can see that it's a dark red because in the days to open a bank account, it's performing badly. However, in the next column, you can see that it's a dark green showing that it actually takes fewer days for the SHG to receive its RF after formation. 

In the next slide, I'll go through conditional formatting options other than color scale very briefly just so you can get a sense of what they all look like and how to apply them. But I'm not going to discuss each of them in detail, and you can come back to this presentation later and look at how all of these are applied and how the rules can be edited to customize it as per your own data requirements. 

Let's see the screen recording to apply different conditional formatting options. Select the data, and we'll first try the Highlight Cell Rules and see what it looks like if you select the Greater Than option. We can change the option to 10%, so it will highlight all the values that are greater than 10%. We can remove the rule by choosing the Clear Rule option. 
Now, let's select the data again to try another type of conditional formatting. Let's go with the Top and Bottom Rules. Let's try highlighting the top 10 items or top 10% of the data and as before you can actually edit the top percentage of what you wanted to be shown as. So, here we want to highlight the top 25%. So, here you can see how it's been highlighted. Again, we'll clear it and I'll show you another option. So, these are the Data Bars but they don't really make sense for our particular type of data, but you can just see how they look. Then is the color scales that we'd seen before, and these are the different icon options that you can also use. And as you're hovering over them, you can see them get applied to the selected data, and you can imagine what they will look like and whether it makes sense for your data. 

You can also set your own rule from scratch and this kind of box will appear if you click the New Formatting Rule option. So, let's select the one which says Format only values that are above or below the average and you can go into the advanced features and decide how your data should appear. So, here I wanted to appear in bold and in red. So, I'll click okay. And now you can see that the values that are above the average have all been highlighted in the red bold formatting that I had selected when I created my own rule. 

So, this brings us to the end of this module on sparklines, columns, and conditional formatting. So, let's go over some limitations of using a table with conditional formatting. 
So, if you're creating and using these conditionally formatted tables in PowerPoint and you're presenting that to an audience, it can be very hard to read, especially because it's not always easy to zoom in to a PowerPoint presentation when you're showing it to an audience. Another point is that your audience may not have enough time to read through the table, especially if it's a detailed table when you're showing it in a presentation. 
And if the conditional formatting that you're using is not explained, the use of colors can also distort your data and mislead your audience. If you're printing the tables and sharing them with people, then the table will not be as impactful if you're only using a black and white printout, especially if you're using the color scale conditional formatting option and you have different colors that are being used to highlight different parts of the data or to mean different things. 
The last point is that the default red and green options that are used in the color scales can be hard to interpret for people who are color blind, because red and green are colors that are especially hard for them to see. And to overcome this, you can actually use the internet to search out color palettes that are suitable for people who are color blind, and that will really help you format your data in a way that's inclusive, and create visualizations that can be read across different types of people with visual impairments so that they can read them clearly and effectively. 

As always, here are some resources that you can use when you're implementing these skills.

And to overcome this, you can actually use the internet to search out color palettes that are suitable for people who are color blind, and that will really help you format your data in a way that's inclusive, and create visualizations that can be read across different types of people with visual impairments so that they can read them clearly and effectively. 00:00 [Music]
00:00 Welcome to the Public Sector Data Science Course, where we teach data-related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 
00:09 In this module on Making Effective Presentations, first part, we'll be looking at an introduction to presentations, deciding the content of a presentation, showing and using data in a presentation, and ending with the basics of presentation design. 
00:27 What is a presentation? A presentation conveys information to an audience using a combination of information and visual elements. Content such as text, images, links, videos etc. can be included in a presentation to deliver useful, consolidated information to a group. Visual elements add to the effectiveness of a presentation and help emphasize the key points being made to the use of type, color, images, videos, graphics, layouts and transitions. 
01:04 So, what are the tools used to make a presentation? Microsoft PowerPoint is the most commonly used tool to make presentations. Other commonly used tools are: Google Slides, Keynote, and Canva. Google Slides is free to use through a Gmail account and your Google Drive or workspace. It runs in your browser with both online and offline compatibility and allows for easy sharing and collaboration. Keynote is a presentation making software developed by Apple and available for free on Apple devices. Canva is an online design platform that lets you use presentation templates to create beautiful looking presentations. The format is a little different to PowerPoint and not all the features are free. In this module, we will primarily discuss PowerPoint, but these same topics can be applied to presentations made across these different tools. In the next module related to presentations, we will also touch upon how Canva can be used to design presentations. 
02:13 Every discussion or meeting does not need a PowerPoint presentation. So, use it when it will enhance the conversation. PowerPoint presentations can be helpful when you want to supplement your discussion with data, visual evidence, combine different types of evidence, present questions for your audience to think about, discuss etc. Some instances where you can use PowerPoint to make a presentation are: review discussions, planning discussions, scheme data analysis and performance discussions and things like that. 
02:50 These three questions can help you decide what all to include in the presentation: What is the objective of the presentation? Who is the audience? What is a potential conclusion/decision? With the objective, be clear about the purpose of the meeting or discussion and what your audience needs to take away from it. In the government setting, the objective of the meeting is usually set in advance and then the PowerPoint and data are prepared, so you already know what has to be discussed. So you can decide to include or not include graphs and slides that are pertinent to that. The audience. Similarly, in a government setting, you will usually already know in advance who all will be attending the meeting. This can help you to decide what all needs to be included. For example, if the senior officer who are you are making the presentation for, and who will be taking the decision is new to the division or scheme, you can include more context or explanation in the slides. Next, potential conclusion or decision. This is also linked with the first two questions. If the objective of the meeting is the budget for the upcoming year, then you know that a concluding discussion will include things like anything from the past year that should or should not have been included or any new proposals or programs that need to be included in the future etc. Keeping these three questions in mind can help to decide what should be included, and also what should not be included in your presentation. As it is best to keep the presentation as short and simple to the point as possible. If you are unsure, you can also decide to keep backup slides at the end of your presentation that you can use in case the topic comes up in discussion. First, decide the content and narrative of the presentation, and then make the slides. Otherwise, the template or design can decide the content instead of the other way around. 
04:53 Keep the text on your slides simple, and use key phrases and include only essential information so as not to clutter your slides too much. Related to that, try not to make more than 5 points per slide. 
05:10 The 2 main ways to show data in a presentation: Table - simplest way of summarizing a set of observations, Charts and graphs - visual representations of numerical data and can convey the general patterns of the data. We discussed both in the Data Visualization modules. The same tables/charts developed in Excel can be used in the presentation. 
05:47 You can create tables and charts directly in PowerPoint or you can add the tables/charts created in Excel into PowerPoint. We will go over how to use both the methods. 
06:04 We will now be discussing the different methods you can use to add data tables to your PowerPoint presentation. The first, you can copy and paste it directly from Excel, second, you can create a table in PowerPoint and then add data to it, third, you can create an embedded Excel sheet for the table, and fourth, you can add a table from Excel with source or destination formatting. In the next slide, let's look at the screen recording on how to go about doing this. 
06:32 [Music] 
08:08 [Music] 
09:03 [Music] 
09:45 Like with Tables, Graphs can also be added through the same methods: Copy & paste directly from Excel, paste with source formatting/embed or destination formatting, Create a table in PowerPoint and then add data. 
10:15 [Music] 
11:56 Let's go over the different methods of adding data that we just saw. The first is adding directly from Excel. The analysis can be conducted separately and then added into PowerPoint which makes it quite easy, and can also allow you to do these processes in parallel or consecutively. If the data is embedded or the table/graph is created within PowerPoint, then the Excel sheet will be accessible to anyone who has the presentation to edit the data. This is a good option when you are working in a team and you're sharing the files over email or WhatsApp or any such other sharing platform. But the flip side to this is that it makes the file quite heavy, and that's something to keep in mind. 
12:44 As we had discussed in the data visualisation module, you should: Ensure graphic has a title, Label the components of your graphic, Indicate source of data with date, Provide number of observations (n=xx) as a reference point, Add footnote if more information is needed. To make your graphics as self-explanatory as possible, there are several things to always include. Every table or graph should have a title or heading. The x and y axis of the graph should be labeled, including value labels such as percentage sign, or you can also include a legend. You should always cite the source of your data and put the date when the data was collected or published. You can provide the sample size, or the number of people to which the graph is referring, that means the n value. And you can include a footnote if the graphic isn't self-explanatory, and these points will preempt questions and explain the data to your audience. In the next several slides, we'll see examples of the points that we just discussed. 
13:37 Once we show the data, we need to interpret the data. Move from ‘what’ is happening in the scheme to ‘why’ it is happening, and ‘how’ we can try to address it. This can begin while you are making the visualisation itself, such as through colours and formatting used or how you use conditional formatting in a table. 
14:05 Data interpretation is the process of making sense of the information. It allows us to ask, what does this information tell me about the program? Here you can see a flowchart of the steps involved in interpreting the data. First is the relevance of the findings, then reasons for the findings, input from other sources, and then lastly, actions to be taken or next steps. Now let's go over these four steps. 
14:34 Some questions which can help to convey the relevance of the data: Does the indicator meet the target? How far from the target is it? How does it compare (to other states, time periods, other programs)? Are there any extreme highs and lows in the data? These should be prepared in advance and discussed while showing the data during the presentation. 
15:03 After the relevant findings have been shown, the next question is what are the potential reasons that are we are seeing this. This answer may not always be easily available, so you can try to: add other data that may provide an answer, supplement with insights from a field visit, consult state/district/block representatives or other experts. 
16:13 Based on the data, relevance and possible explanations, the presentation should head towards discussing the next steps to be taken. 
16:36 Like how we just showed how the data presented should show the relevance, reasons, inputs and next steps, the same way the entire presentation should also flow like a story. The narrative should make sense from the view of the objective of the meeting and the scheme/programme being discussed. 
17:00 For example, a scheme/programme review presentation can generally follow this order: 
17:24 Use a simple template, Use dark coloured text on a light background (like in this presentation) or light coloured text on a dark background, Avoid using patterns and shading. 
18:02 Try to use the same font throughout, Readable font size, Different fonts/sizes/text colour to place emphasis. 
18:29 Don't use more than 3 colours in your presentation, Try to use the same colour for text across the slides to create uniformity, Similarly, use your chosen colour theme for Smart Art and charts/graphs and use contrasting colours to highlight. 
18:56 This brings us to the end of this module. In the next part we'll be discussing themes and templates, diagrams and SmartArt and the basics of Canva, an online tool for presentations.

This is the Public Sector Data Science Course where we teach data-related skills that are useful in the government context in India. 

In this module on Normalisation of indicators, we'll go through: why we need to normalise to compare data, then standardisation or Z-scores, then we'll look at rescaling using Min-Max normalisation, and end with some discussion on selecting a method for normalisation.

Like with previous modules, we'll use the example of a task to go through the steps. Imagine this is an assignment that you have been given by your reporting officer. You've been asked by your reporting officer to create an index to track state performance in MGNREGA such that they do not need to refer to rankings across different indicators to understand overall performance. This is the same task that was given in the previous few modules and after the steps followed in those, now we have to normalise the indicators that have already been selected for the index.

If you remember the previous modules, we'd gone through the overall steps to create a composite index. Now we will look at the third step, which is the normalisation of indicators. 

These were the indicators that we had selected through the previous modules. So the first column has State, which has the names of the states. The second one, the first indicator is the percentage of job cards issued out of people who had applied for job cards. Then is persondays of employment provided per household employed. Then is the work completion rate. Next is the percentage of transactions completed within stage one, which is within 15 days. Then is the percentage of SC/ST workers out of total active workers. And then the last one is percentage of Gram Panchayats that have completed at least one social audit in that particular financial year. So we'll proceed with these indicators. 

Now, if you look at all the indicators that we just went through, you will see that they represent different things or have different units, such as persondays, work completion rate, number of households completing 100 days of employment, or even percentage of Gram Panchayats that have done at least one social audit. So how can we make these different indicators comparable? And the way that we can do that is through normalisation. 

Normalisation is usually used to make different indicators in a composite index comparable. It is required when indicators have different measurement scales or they are expressed in different units. Different types of normalisation can be applied, such as: standardisation or Z-scores, or rescaling (0 to 1) or min-max normalisation. Normalising presents the different indicators as per the same scale or range, and this makes them comparable. It helps to prevent one indicator from being overly influential in the composite index. 

In this module, we'll discuss two types of normalisation. The first will be standardisation using Z-scores, and the second will be min-max (0 to 1) normalisation. 

What is standardisation or Z-score? Standardisation converts the distribution of scores in the indicator to a standard normal distribution. This means that after standardisation the mean of the scores will be 0 and the standard deviation will be 1. If all the different indicators that we plan to include are standardised, the mean for all will be 0 and the standard deviation will be 1. Thus making the different indicators comparable. 

If you can think back to the module that we had done on descriptive and summary statistics, then you will remember the detailed discussions that we had about the mean, median, and the standard deviations. So we'll draw on those concepts and the same Excel functions that we used there to perform this process of standardisation. So essentially here we have visualized the process that you will go through. We'll take the set of data that looks like the curve on the left and normalize it to the curve on the right, where the median is 0 and the standard deviation is 1. 

We can standardise scores in Excel using the STANDARDIZE function:
= STANDARDIZE (x, mean, standard deviation)
Here x is the value that has to be normalised. This refers to the mean of the distribution that has to be normalised. This can be calculated using the Excel AVERAGE function. This refers to the standard deviation of the distribution that has to be normalised. This can be calculated using the Excel function STDEV.P. 

The first step will be to calculate the mean and standard deviations for both the data you want to standardize using the Excel functions AVERAGE and STDEV.P. So let's look at the screen recording on how to go about doing this. 

So now for the first indicator that we want to normalize, we start the average function for the mean, and then the standard deviation function and again we select the same range of data for that indicator. Now for the second indicator, again we calculate the average for the entire one thing and then the standard deviation as well, and that's fairly simple. Now in the next screen recording, we'll see how we can use the mean and standard deviation that we've already calculated, and plug those in to the standardisation function to calculate the Z-scores for these two indicators. 

So you'll start by typing STANDARDIZE, open the bracket, we'll select the first number that you need to normalize, select the mean, and then select the standard deviation. So now because we want to drag and apply this formula to the entire list, we'll use the dollar signs to fix those particular values. And as you draw it down, you can see the formula has been applied. Similarly for the next indicator, again you do STANDARDIZE, apply it, and as you drag it down throughout, all of the values will get normalized. 

The Z-scores will appear as shown here: 
And to check if the Z-scores do indeed fall into a standard normal distribution, you can calculate the mean and standard deviation for the Z-scores and you will see that the mean is 0 and standard deviation is 1.
